Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to participate in the debate on Eldorado Nuclear. I am sorry that one of the government Members has decided that there needs to be an elimination of further debate by moving to prevent additional amendments to the Bill.
I want to deal with a couple of matters. One is the question of privatization, and the second is the impact of privatization as it relates to the handling of nuclear waste, be it low level or high level.
I had the opportunity both as a Member of Parliament and as a member of the provincial legislature of Ontario to deal with the matter of low level nuclear waste being stored in the Port Hope area and I was able to meet with citizens concerned about the existence of a dump so close to a major water body.
The people see quite realistically that although they have had difficulty getting a Crown corporation to move the dump away from their source of drinking water, they fear, legitimately, that a privately owned company would be even less responsive than a government owned one. When we have commodities such as uranium and its by-products, I do not think we should follow what the Americans do, which is to leave it to private profit enterprise to handle and manage this volatile fuel, a fuel that has well known, well documented dangers to the health and safety of those who come near it whether in its fuel or in its waste form. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on the Environment and Forestry tabled an excellent report. That committee reviewed the whole nuclear waste cycle and made a number of recommendations to the Government as to how it should approach the issue. The privatization of Eldorado flies in the face of the intent of that report and flies in the face of sound economic management of a company that is using as its energy source a volatile material. It is wrong for that reason.
Then we have the whole concept of privatization as embodied by the Conservative Government of Canada. It is really difficult for the Government to accept the reality that you can actually have a publicly owned, that is, a taxpayer owned company, that can be efficient and profitable and that does not need to draw on the taxpayers of Canada to sustain it. The Government for years has preached that the private sector is the only sector that can do that, that public Crown corporations do not work and are a socialist evil. Whether it is Eldorado Nuclear, Air Canada or any other Crown corporation in this country, Canada has a tradition of where there is a public need the Government has the responsibility to ensure that all of us own it.
Where in Canada over our history have we had for any length of time privately owned hydroelectricity distribution systems? The vast majority of them are publicly owned. I come from a community in part of the country that has gone beyond the electricity aspect and has got into the telephone company business. We have Sask Tel, Alberta Tel, the City of Thunder Bay telephone company, and the Kenora telephone

company-all are publicly owned, profit making companies that are able to keep rates down.
Let us look at Air Canada. We have in Air Canada a company that has not cost the taxpayers a cent in 25 years. In fact, in the last 11 years, its after-tax profit has been in the magnitude of $450 million. It is an efficient company. It provides a public good. It gives the Government of Canada and therefore the people of Canada a window into the industry to help shape policies in a deregulated environment. What is wrong with that? What is wrong with every taxpayer having a share in Air Canada? Every man, woman and child who lives in Canada and is a Canadian citizen does in fact own Air Canada, Eldorado Nuclear and all the other Crown corporations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of points with regard to the Eldorado privatization legislation which is before the House. Eldorado as a Crown corporation has been able to carry out a very important role in regional development. The federal Government located some of its refining facilities at Blind River, Ontario. As well, it has undertaken important developmental activity in Saskatchewan and has located a refinery and upgrading facility in Port Hope.
Crown corporations play a dual role. They play a role of economic development, job creation and wealth generation and they also play a national role in developing regional economies. When we privatize an industry of this type, we must be sure that commitments which have been made by the Crown corporation to the municipalities and communities involved are honoured by the company that will succeed Eldorado.
This may seem like a small thing in the global context of a corporation which will have assets of $1.6 billion and annual sales of $500 million, but those commitments which have been made to the communities are of vital importance. They are
important to the communities' over-all social activities, the organization of the communities and their recreational facilities. They are important as well to the economic viability of the communities.
For instance, in the Town of Blind River, Eldorado established a uranium refinery in 1983-84 and made commitments to provide certain leases to the town at nominal rates for recreational facilities such as a campground and a golf course. In the case of the golf course, I believe that the lease is $1 per year for 100 acres or so of land. That golf course was developed in co-operation with the town. I am sure there are similar kinds of arrangements in Port Hope as well.
The people of these communities want to be sure that when the company is amalgamated with the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation, those commitments will be honoured. If they are not, then clearly I as an elected representative cannot and would not support this divestiture and privatization of the corporation. It would simply be breaking a legally binding commitment.
There are other commitments as well. For instance, Blind River built a recreational facility which carries a debt of some $1.2 million, I understand, and Eldorado Resources has made a commitment of a grant of some 60 per cent for recreational facilities in lieu of taxes. The details of this tend to be rather technical, but it is a very real benefit for the Town of Blind River. This past year, the grant for recreational facilities was some $85,000. That figure is prorated on the basis of the grant in lieu of taxes. Certainly we on this side of the House, and I am sure the Hon. Member from the Port Hope area, if there are similar arrangements with that community and perhaps areas in the West as well, want a commitment that at committee stage those arrangements, such as in the case of the community recreation facility in Blind River, will be honoured if and when the amalgamated company is sold to the private sector. If not, Blind River will be thrown into complete financial disarray because that commitment could not easily be picked up by the local taxpayers. The town's industrial base is practically just the uranium refinery there.
I think over-all this privatization-amalgamation with SMDC can be a positive thing. SMDC has always tried to get an exemption for further refining and upgrading in this country. If it is concerned about the long-term benefit to that corporation, it will want under this arrangement, to see uranium refined as well as mined in this country.
The amalgamated companies will have extensive low-cost reserves and will be well able to compete on the world stage. That strength will help in the further refining and upgrading part of the company. Unfortunately, in the free trade deal the Government has given away our upgrading policy in many areas, including uranium. It wants to drive our country back to being hewers of wood and drawers of water. This amalgamation will partially compensate for that because SMDC will
April 18, 1988

obviously want to do its refining in Canada when it amalgamates with the only company with uranium refining and upgrading facilities.
In conclusion, I hope those concerns relating to the communities where Eldorado has facilities will be taken into account. Clearly we will be looking very closely at the Bill in committee to ensure that those legally binding commitments are honoured not only by the Government of the day but by Eldorado Resources and the new company being created. We want to see those commitments and binding obligations carried forward to the new privatized corporation.

maintopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to join in this debate on Bill C-121. I am glad to have the opportunity to raise some questions about this proposal to take a vitally important company, one of the most important developments in mining and processing which the 20th century has witnessed, and have it pass out of the immediate control of the Government of Canada through a Crown corporation.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), judging by the tenor of his observations this morning, has accepted this situation. In my remarks I would like to reject that outcome and consider good reasons why the proposal the Government has put before us should be rejected by this House. In that way we will ensure that Eldorado Nuclear continues as one of Canada's Crown corporations in order to achieve a number of desirable economic, social, and, if you will, political goals for the Canadian people.
One might of course ask at the outset why it is necessary to privatize Eldorado Nuclear. Our Conservative Government would still, I suppose, pride itself on being one of a long tradition of Conservative Governments concerned about the development of Canada's resources in order to provide economic development and other gains for the Canadian people. Given that, the Canadian people might well ask the Government for its reason for the decision to privatize in this particular area. Surely it is not sufficient simply to think that ideology should govern in any of these matters. I do not think the Canadian people are ever impressed when the only reason a Party has for doing something is that that is what the Party program says. They want to be convinced that the Party program makes sense for them. I know the Conservatives will be very good at making that kind of criticism of items in the NDP program, so it seems to me more than fair to ask the same kinds of questions of the Conservative Government.
Why privatize something that was created during the 1940s as a vital instrument to ensure that uranium would be available for war purposes and then turned to more peaceful purposes later on? I make that comment to remind Canadians that there can be no doubt about our involvement with the nuclear age and our responsibility for the use of atomic weapons, or our role in the way in which the use of nuclear weapons has developed in this century, particularly in the
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
United States. Canadians have been involved both directly and indirectly.
Given that reality, it made sense to have a Crown corporation do this. Is there now any reason at all to turn away and put it out to the private sector? Surely one can summon any number of reasons. I know my friends and colleagues speaking before me in this debate, having 20 minutes to respond to this Bill, have provided abundant reasons why Eldorado Nuclear should remain a Crown corporation, why this kind of flotation should not be carried out.
The Government has decided that holding the shares on behalf of the people of Canada is the way to go. Having questioned that decision on behalf of the people of Canada we might look to the others involved in this company, those who work for it, those who are represented by the United Steel Workers and by the Energy and Chemical Workers. We might well ask them whether it makes sense to carry through this privatization.
The media have been having a great deal of fun in the last days asking Air Canada employees whether privatization of our national air carrier makes sense. Of course, the fun has been that a certain number of Air Canada employees have said that it is a great idea. It is significant that in the case of Eldorado Nuclear such support does not exist. The two unions involved have listed a number of very good reasons for being opposed to this particular proposal. They have pointed to concerns about occupational health and safety. They have raised concerns about the environmental problems which uranium mining and processing create in the areas in which it is carried on. They have, of course, the most natural reason for being concerned about jobs as well.
I would think that everyone knows that the mining and processing of uranium involves very real dangers to those who do it and to the places in which it is carried on. In fact, concerns about health and about the environment are profoundly interrelated. We have here, after all, some of the most insidious dangers to life of all sorts that the late 19th century has to offer. Those who did the initial research-and one thinks of Madame Curie who carried out research on radiation without realizing what it could do-very often died a terrible and early death because of the lack of knowledge of its consequences.
The concern about health in the processing of uranium is one which private corporations can all too easily dodge. A Crown corporation should have the highest standards, and Eldorado Nuclear should be maintained as a Crown corporation to ensure that Canadians remain state of the art in terms of occupational health and safety in the mining and processing of uranium.
With regard to the environmental concerns rising before us, at the Port Hope refinery we have enormous quantities of tailings. The dump is practically full and the disposal problem

April 18, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
gets larger and larger in an area which is all too close to the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence system. We have disposal problems in other areas as well.
Not immediately related, but as a consequence of the way in which we use the nuclear age to produce electric power, we have additional waste disposal problems. Atomic Energy of Canada has been involved for years in trying to come to grips with these questions. Surely it would be far better to support and supplement the endeavours of AECL by maintaining Eldorado Nuclear as a Crown corporation equipped to do the work that is necessary and ensure that the environmental concerns of so many Canadians will be provided for adequately.
The occupational health and safety and environmental concerns which the unions have expressed and so many Canadians believe exist are powerful arguments against the proposal the Government has put forward.
In the area of jobs the Government may provide fine assurances that there will be continued employment in the mining and processing of uranium, but the reality is that there is no real guarantee given. In an era of over-production, of difficulties of controlling and managing supply in order to maintain prices that allow the industry some small amount of profit, activities that created enormous difficulties for Canada when a legal process was begun in the United States against the cartel-like arrangements that were involved in this argue all the more for careful involvement with the industry rather than hiving it off on the private sector to have Lord-knows-what happen.
If the Conservative Government, in utter irresponsibility, in rejection of all the concerns-the public concerns, the workers' concerns, and the public interest that I have been sketching- wanted to dispose of the whole area, simply get itself out from under it, there might be a case for looking at that, although it would strike everyone as completely irresponsible. However, this particular proposal is not as clear-cut as that. We are going to see a flotation of stock in the best stock promoter tradition of the capital markets of this country and other countries of the world. We are going to see an attempt to sell stock in order to bring in capital for Eldorado.
How is that going to be facilitated? How does the Government want to encourage investors to buy the stock? It is going to do that by ensuring that the new company resulting from the reorganization of the Saskatchewan Mining Development Corporation and Eldorado Nuclear is not burdened with debt, and particularly not burdened with the expenses which may well ensue at Port Hope as the environmental control and tailings disposal problems arise and someone is forced to deal with them. Those who buy the stock of this new company will be spared all of those problems because the Government of Canada intends to shoulder the larger part of the cost.
There, of course, is the most atrocious kind of privatization which the Conservative Government has carried through a number of times-tempt someone into control of a new
enterprise, or an old enterprise transformed in this way, turn it over to them, make it tempting for them, offer them the chance to profit by leaving all the costs with the Canadian taxpayer. Take from the Government of Canada the possibility of future profits and give those to others. Leave the burden of the costs on the Canadian taxpayer. That surely, Mr. Speaker, is the final stupidity in this kind of privatization.
It is for those reasons that I join with my colleagues in firmly opposing the Government's proposal in Bill C-121.

the private sector is that there is a real problem in the Conservative caucus. The Neanderthals on the back bench are tugging at the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), telling him to put the Government back into what they believe are the true blue Conservative colours. In the 1940s the Government established declaratory powers with respect to uranium. The Government of the day recognized the importance of uranium and therefore brought Eldorado into the public sector. While resources are a provincial jurisdiction according to the Constitution of Canada, uranium became a federal responsibility because the Government recognized the importance of having direct control over the exploitation of that resource. As a result of moving in and establishing Eldorado Nuclear, the federal Government and the people of Canada had a direct control over this particular resource. The federal Government is responsible for this resource and its jurisdiction is clear. Parliament can hold the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources responsible and accountable for the exploitation and the research and development of uranium which is part of Eldorado's mandate.
The Government is going to privatize Eldorado. In doing so, where does it leave the taxpayers? I have already said that the Government is removing its direct control over this particular company. Furthermore, the taxpayers of Canada will keep the debt. The buyers get the gravy and we get the scraps.

maintopic: ELDORADO NUCLEAR LIMITED REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising today to address Bill C-121 and further motions on it, I must express my grave concerns as the environment critic for my Party. The previous Member talked about the money aspect of this deal and the total unfairness for the Canadian public since the privatization deal will mean profits to the private industry and responsibility and costs to be left to the public sector. As well, the cost of long term clean-up and waste disposal problems are left with the people of Canada. That is certainly unfair.
If privatization meant that companies would become more responsible in this industry and, looking at the long-term costs, would decide that it is not an industry in their best interest from the point of view of profits, I would be in favour of privatization. I would favour it if I thought it would result in environmental improvement, improved health for Canadians and more sanity in an area where we as a society have made mistakes in the past.
That does not exist with Bill C-121. It is a very misguided Bill which will not have the same results as we have seen happening in the United States where nuclear facilities are either being closed down or planned ones not opening because of the enormous costs and the fact that profits will evaporate in an industry which entails such danger. There is also the possibility of law suits, spills, melt-downs, and so on which would certainly discourage private facilities in the United States. However, we will not have any of those disincentives with Bill C-121. Instead of talking about privatization, we should really be talking about environment and health and whether this is a safe industry for Canadians in the first place. If we thought it was safe, and I think the answer to that is no, the question would be, would it produce as many jobs as using other energy sources? We would certainly find the answer to that is, no, that we would do much better in terms of job creation and safety of communities in Canada if we went a different route.
I do want to spend a little time in dealing with a problem within Eldorado Nuclear itself. All Members of Parliament will have received a letter from the Port Granby Monitoring Committee. I would like to read a couple of paragraphs into the record. They read:
We are writing this letter to you to enlist your help with a very serious problem. Eldorado Resources Limited, a Crown corporation, has been operating a nuclear dump right on the edge of Lake Ontario since 1952.
The Port Granby dump is leaky, ill conceived and a potential disaster, a fact which is not unrecognized by various experts and authorities who have examined this dump site.
Indeed, the danger of the situation has been recognized for a very long time. We are talking about Lake Ontario from which 2.5 million Canadians get their drinking water. We are not talking about some obscure place unconnected to any major waterways. There are no obscure places unconnected to major

April 18, 1988
Eldorado Nuclear Limited
waterways in Canada. Our water is connected by stream and underground river. The letter goes on to say:
In 1976, the Atomic Energy Control Board (AECB) issued a press release recognizing that the site is a problem and decided that the dump was to be decommissioned as of January 1977.
This has not been done.
In 1978, a panel of experts examined all aspects of a proposed refinery and permanent dump site in Port Granby and decided that neither the refinery nor a dump should be located in Port Granby.
This was decided for all kinds of good reasons. This is what the experts had been saying. But this dump site is still in use. The licence expires at the end of April this year and we do not know whether it will be renewed. We do not know what is going to happen. We do not even know what rights citizens will have to participate in the decision-making because the procedures under the Atomic Energy Control Board are very sloppy. Citizens do not have clear rights. They fare somewhat better before other regulatory bodies, but the AECB is one which has not remotely recognized the need for citizen participation. AECB has ordered plans for decommissioning, but this dump site is still in use and, possibly by the end of this month, it will be licensed for further ongoing use.
In the meantime a task force was established on the principles of establishing a site for dumping. The task force set out the kinds of criteria which meant that Port Granby would not be chosen. Indeed, it is hard to imagine what communities might be chosen because the task force set very strict criteria. Unfortunately, it did propose to let communities bid for the honour of being a nuclear dump site. I say "unfortunately" because perhaps there is no alternative. It considered that there might be communities which are so desperate for jobs that they would be prepared to take this on because there would be some income coming into the community.
The issue of the Port Granby dump site actually became a subject in the last election campaign. I have a letter dated August 21, 1984, and everyone in the House will remember the time in August of 1984 as being at the height of the election campaign. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the then Leader of the Opposition, an aspirant for the Office of Prime Minister, wrote to the Port Hope community saying:
Thank you for your letter outlining your concern about the proposed permanent disposal site for low-level radioactive waste in the vicinity of Wesleyville, Ontario.
He pointed out that this had been contested for a very long time and that the proposals by Eldorado Nuclear for establishing a permanent radioactive waste disposal dump either near Port Granby or Wesleyville were not acceptable to the people of those communities. He further stated:
All such waste should be removed from major population areas and kept well away from any major resource such as Lake Ontario.
Let us look to the fine print of this message. It is fine if one lives on Lake Ontario, and after all Toronto is on Lake Ontario and we would not want to have some kind of leakage which would affect a large population, but if one lives in a
smaller community, further away and not on Lake Ontario, on some smaller lake, then it is all right. They do not want to bump off millions of people with some kind of nuclear disaster, but what is wrong with hundreds or thousands? There is a notion that as long as it is moved away from major centres, perhaps it is all right. What that means is that people are dispensable. If they are in small enough numbers we can ignore them. They can be left out of consideration completely. I think it is highly immoral to think that if it is only a small number of people who will get leukemia, or a small number of women who will bear children with birth defects, that somehow that is acceptable. The Prime Minister pointed out:
While this would involve greater expense, the federal Government, as owner of the Eldorado Nuclear Limited, must accept at least partial responsibility and provide the leadership.
Well, what the Government is doing now is moving to privatization and simply ignoring the ongoing problem, and that is something the public will have to pay for with their lives and with their quality of life. The Prime Minister concluded:
I appreciate being advised of your concern about this matter which, I know, is shared by many Canadians. You can be assured that a Progressive Conservative Government will work most actively towards a safe, acceptable and permanent storage arrangement for all hazardous wastes.
This is beautiful language, "safe, acceptable and permanent storage arrangement for all hazardous wastes". But that does not exist. We do not have safe methods of disposal for low-level or high-level radioactive waste. The Standing Committee on the Environment and Forestry, in the case of high-level radioactive waste, recommended a moratorium on nuclear facilities until we have a safe and affordable method of disposal. Yet there are even more low-level radioactive wastes than high-level in Canada. Quantitatively, it is a greater problem even considering the disproportion in the effect it may have, because we have millions of tonnes of low-level radioactive waste. We have had mining for a long time. The material has not been dealt with adequately and this problem will continue.
I simply point out that we have an enormous environmental and health problem with which to deal. The high sounding words of the Prime Minister do not help us to solve the problem because they do not recognize that the problem exists and we do not have a solution. That is what we should be talking about.
The question of privatization has to be dealt with within the context of what we are talking about. We are not talking about a cookie factory. We are talking about an outfit that mines and processes uranium into nuclear products, either military or non-military. We are talking about a product for which we have as yet no safe means of disposal. We are talking about a product that requires safe disposal for thousands of years. The problem is serious. The Government is not dealing with the environmental consequences and, therefore, I urge the House to send this Bill back so we can really look at the environmental questions which are absolutely critical.
April 18, 1988

Mr. Speaker, as I understand it we are now on Bill C-l 17, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. This was introduced into the House on March 22 and combines a number of provisions announced in the 1987-88 budgets and a number of the tax reform items in the June and December Ways and Means resolutions which were put before the House. The most current item from the point of view of Canadians is the implementation just a week ago of the excise tax on gasoline amounting to 1 cent a litre. Although this occurred during the week of April 1, it certainly was no small April Fool's joke for Canadians.
It is interesting that in the Ways and Means resolution we have tax adjustments which provide for the reduction of tariffs of some $460 million in the first full calendar year under the trade agreement between Canada and the United States. In those same Budget Papers there is provision for a reduction in tariffs of some $55 million in the first three months of 1989. This Ways and Means resolution taxpaper suggests that the increase in revenues generated by the Government of Canada from the excise tax provision included in Bill C-l 17 will raise, I believe, some $300 million in the second year and some $275 million in the first year. Those figures indicate some of the problems of the free trade agreement. The Government would have us believe that the equivalent of 1 cent a litre will give us massive new access to the United States market. It is hard to believe that the equivalent of tariffs of that amount will give us that massive new access. In fact, it is unbelievable.
When we look at the tariffs under the trade deal we see that 80 per cent of everything that goes into the United States goes in tax-free or tariff-free already. The tax tariffs involve only 5 per cent, on the balance of 15 per cent on which item there are tariffs. We see a trade-off there of the Government imposing an excise tax of 1 cent a litre to pay for the loss of the tariffs from the free trade deal.
These revenues raised under the Excise Tax Act through Bill C-l 17 are some of the tools used by the Government to create a smoke and mirrors illusion that the deficit has been reduced. If so, the deficit has been decreased at the expense of the average Canadian's wallet.

April 18, 1988

The Government's proposition that it will reduce the deficit level is really hard to believe. If we look at the list of taxation items which the Government has imposed on Canadians since 1984, it is devastating. It reads like one of the largest taxation grabs in our history. I believe that in the first two and a half years it involved some $22 billion. Most Canadians hardly notice these things because they are so constant. The increase we had last week in gasoline tax will raise $300 million.
The tax levied on January 1 will raise hundreds of millions of dollars. The sales tax, without getting into the new sales tax planned by the Minister, which will apply to everything from getting your car fixed to getting your hair cut, has raised hundreds of millions and billions of dollars because the Government has increased the sales tax by some 25 per cent from 9 per cent to 12 per cent in its first two and a half years in office. To look over the list of taxes, let alone the excise tax on gasoline, is a frightening prospect for Canadians. People often come to me and ask, "What are you guys doing down there? Every time I have been able, through my union, to get an increase in my pay of 3 per cent, 4 per cent or 5 per cent over the last three or four years, I don't have any more take-home pay". That is the problem of the Government having deindexed the income tax schedules. The Government has imposed every conceivable kind of tax on Canadians.
This Bill provides for some taxes in 1987 and 1988. Let us look at the list of taxes from 1984 to 1988. The first sales tax of 1 per cent was imposed in the fall of 1984, which increased taxes for Canadians by $1 billion. The second one was imposed via the sales tax in 1986, which increased the sales tax by another $1 billion. The third increase of 1 per cent in sales tax in 1986 raised another billion dollars.
Looking at the increases in gasoline tax, the first increase of 2 cents a litre was imposed in 1985, and it raised $930 million. The second increase of one cent per litre on gas occurred in 1987 and raised $450 million. The third increase of one cent per litre on gas in 1987 raised $450 million. Those are just excise taxes and sales taxes which have been imposed since the Government came to power.
The equalization of the sales tax on unleaded versus leaded gasoline in 1987 raised another $30 million. The extension of the sales tax to candy, soft drinks and pet foods in 1985 raised $400 million. Just think, we are even imposing taxes on children's confections and soft drinks and on pet food. There was then an extension of the sales tax to snack food in 1987, raising $60 million.
The first increase on cigarettes and tobacco taxes in 1985 raised $320 million. That was in direct defiance of the promises of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) who made a solid, binding commitment that there would be no new taxes on cigarettes and tobacco because of the adverse impact they would have on the tobacco farmers of southwestern Ontario. There was then a deliberate, planned, calculated increase
Excise Tax Act
designed to hurt those hard-pressed tobacco farmers of southwestern Ontario.
As if that were not enough, there was another increase of taxes on tobacco and alcohol in 1986, raising $150 million. There was a third increase of 4 per cent on tobacco taxes in 1987, increasing taxes by some $70 million.
The elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan occurred in 1985 at a time when there was a shortage of affordable housing in many areas of southern Ontario. The Government took away that program, not only increasing taxes by $105 million but making things impossible for young couples who were just starting out and had been saving to be able to buy a home. That ability was snatched away from them by a Government hell-bent on raising taxes but not actually reducing the deficit by any appreciable amount.
The deindexation of the taxation system in 1986 increased taxes by $635 million. The elimination of the federal tax reduction in 1986 had the impact of increasing taxes by $650 million. The changes to the marital exemptions in 1986 imposed an additional $20 million in taxes.
The general 3 per cent surtax change which occurred in 1986 is costing Canada a whopping $1.2 billion, the largest single tax increase since the Government came to power. The temporary 5 per cent and 10 per cent surtaxes of 1986 raised $500 million, creating a greater burden of taxes on Canadians.
An increase in the airport transportation tax in 1987 has required travellers to pay an extra $45 million. The 10 per cent tax on long-distance phone calls and cable services effective January 1 is imposing some $945 million in taxes on Canadians. That particular tax measure is seen by many Canadians, and particularly those who live in rural areas, as being a tax on rural Canada and on the regions. It is also a tax on older people because they are often the ones who make long-distance calls to their children and their grandchildren who live across Canada.
We know that there already is a very high taxation rate on long-distance calls, and this new tax only makes it worse. Some small businessmen from my constituency find that this raises a major new cost for them, an additional cost of up to $100 per month. This is a tax which they cannot afford to pay.
We know that long-distance charges already carry a larger burden of the cost of phone services of almost $1 billion because more charges are put on long-distance calls than on monthly charges for individual telephones. The rate structure of the CRTC has, over the years, put the additional cost on long-distance charges rather than on the hand-sets in homes.
The last item on the list I have here of tax increases the Government has implemented in the last three and a half devastating years of tax increases is the taxation on paint, wallpaper, toys and handicrafts. The Government has taxed everything in sight before the election, even to the point of taxing the wallpaper and paint used in our homes and our toys and handicrafts. This increase amounts to $370 million.

Excise Tax Act
This is a very harsh and destructive tale of tax increases, some of which are to be implemented by Bill C-117. We see this as being an ongoing approach. The Government just dealt with the divestiture of Eldorado Nuclear, and through that we see the Government reaching out to get its hands on another $4 million, $5 million or $6 million which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will use if and when the deal goes through to the private sector to try to make the Budget look good. At the same time as the debt will be left with the federal Government, the available cash from that deal will go into the Government's current Budget.
Of course, the Minister of Finance did the same thing with Teleglobe Canada. That sale of some $500 million or $600 million was used last year in an attempt to get the budget deficit for the year below $30 billion. That comes on top of the hit list of at least $22 billion in tax increases for the average Canadian. Everything from the indexation of income tax rolls to toys, handicrafts, pet foods and non-prescription drugs has come under the hammer of this Minister of Finance in his quest for more taxes.
I spoke of the deficit of $29.3 billion that the Government has sustained in its last Budget. The Government was able to get the deficit down below the magical figure of the Minister of Finance through the sale of Teleglobe and other Crown corporations. I suppose that Air Canada will be the next item which will be used to generate revenues while leaving the national debt untouched and making the deficit for the current year's financing drop below that figure of $30 billion.
It bears repeating that one of the ways this illusion was created was through the use of accounting tricks such as acceleration of tax remittances. Employers who deduct income tax, unemployment insurance premiums and Canada Pension Plan contributions from their employees have been required to do it earlier and with greater frequency since 1987. Employers had been remitting once a month, but in January of that year they had to start remitting twice a month. It is this kind of trickery that the Government used to try to get the deficit below the $30 billion mark. That does not really fool Canadians. It just shows how desperate the Government is to look good even though the facts say otherwise.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity tb comment on the speech given by the Hon. Member on Bill C-117 which the Government suddenly sprung on the House. The uncertainty that characterizes the Government is never more clear than in the planning of House business.
The Hon. Member represents a riding at the other end of Lake Superior and has done so for a good many years now as a member of the Liberal caucus. I would like to have him comment on some of the particular consequences the tax
measures of the Conservative Government have for our constituents in northern Ontario. I am thinking particularly of the several increases in the tax on gasoline, which he said something about. I would also like him to refer to the impact of the 10 per cent telecommunications tax which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) so kindly gave Canadians who have to use the telephone to keep in touch and do business. The combination of those two taxes could be very serious indeed for our constituents in northern Ontario.
We can easily appreciate that persons in Metropolitan Toronto, for example, where the Minister of Finance has his own political base, are able to make all kinds of business calls without running into the kinds of charges that constituents in my riding and, I expect, in his, face. Our constituents who do business with people in the large cities have to pay long-distances charges. To have this tax laid on top is just another burden. I recognize that in the resource industries we sometimes have pretty good wage rates, but in comparison with what one can do in Metropolitan Toronto I would not think our constituents have much to boast about on the income side. To have these taxes loaded on them is really a very heavy burden.
The Hon. Member represents a riding where the Liberal Party has had strength for a long time. We NDP and the Liberals will be wrestling in northern Ontario again to see how many seats we can win there. It is going to be a pleasure to see the Conservatives bite the dust in some of those ridings which they happened to win in 1984 or a little earlier for just the kinds of reasons we see in this Bill. It spares the people in the metropolitan areas, who can make business calls without longdistance charges or who can ride the subway to work, those expenses that our constituents face in Thunder Bay-Nipigon, Algoma, and the other northern Ontario ridings.

Mr. Speaker, I could not have put it better myself. The Hon. Member has raised the inequity of the Government's fiscal policy as it relates to the regions.
If we look at the impact of the several Budgets the Minister of Finance has brought in, we find that he has imposed at least a four cent a litre increase in the tax on gasoline. That is almost 20 cents a gallon. We recall that the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), when he was Minister of Finance and brought in his Budget in 1979, went down the drain by imposing an 18 cent a gallon tax on gasoline. Clearly 20 cents a gallon will be enough to break the Government's back in the next election, certainly in regions like northern Ontario.
This is not only a regressive tax for northern Ontario, it is regressive for every low-income person in this country. The person earning $100,000 a year probably lives in a big urban centre anyway and can certainly afford that 20 cents a gallon much easier than the low-income person who maybe has to drive 10 or 15 miles a day to work because he lives in a rural area. He lives there because he cannot afford a home in the urban centre. That of course is just doubled and tripled for
April 18, 1988

everyone living in areas like northern Ontario, northern Quebec, the Prairies and other regions.
This gas tax is extremely regressive and is part of the overall scheme of the Government to get away from the graduated income tax. It is always interesting to hear the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) saying that with tax reform we are going to take 850,000 Canadians off the tax rolls. What they do not say is that they have put over a million people on the tax rolls by deindexing income tax rates, and are taking millions of dollars away from them when they buy their gas. The sales tax has been increased by 25 per cent as well. That applies to non-prescription drugs, confectionery products, even pet foods. All this will impact much more heavily on low-income Canadians.
The Hon. Member mentioned the telecommunications tax. We already pay extremely high long-distance charges. Over the years the CRTC skewed the rate structure for Bell Canada and other telephone companies so that the basic service charge is relatively low and long-distance charges are high. It is skewed by about $1 billion. What do we find out on January 1? It is skewed by another $1 billion. This is not something that built up over a period of time, it went boom in last year's Budget.
That impacts especially on small businesses. I am familiar with one small business in Little Current, Ontario, a marina. They wrote to me and said they just cannot afford this. It is an extra tax of almost $100 a month on the operation of the business. They are in a rural area far away from the sources of supply. As the Hon. Member indicated, the impact is very adverse for the regions of our country like northern Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has totally bungled the issues of the St. Pierre and Miquelon boundary and the French fishing quotas. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has failed to take these matters seriously. In a letter to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
(Mr. Siddon) dated August 29, 1986, the Prime Minister wrote:
I agree that in dealing with this sensitive issue we must weigh, on the one
hand, the interests of Canadian fishermen and fishing communities and, on the
other hand, our bilateral relations with France.
This policy was fundamentally wrong. The interests of our fishermen should have been the foremost priority. It is no wonder that the Atlantic fishing industry strongly condemned the agreement reached in January, 1987.
What is the state of our bilateral relations with France now? In response to the arrest of a boat apprehended for illegally fishing in our waters, the French Government has recalled its Ambassador. Canadian travellers are now being harassed by the French at border points. I hope that now, finally, the federal Government and the Prime Minister will give this matter the serious attention it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, during this National Citizenship Week all Canadians should reflect on one of the most fundamental aspects of our citizenship, namely, the rich multicultural diversity of our society. Citizenship in Canada means acceptance of difference, tolerance of difference, and celebration of the richness that this diversity has brought to our nation.
I believe that the positive approach to preserving our linguistic and cultural diversity is one of the things that sets us apart among nations. It is worth preserving. It is an integral part of our concept of citizenship. By living together and working together in harmony we can provide an example for all people and enrich our own lives as well.
Citizenship Week provides a real opportunity for all of us to reflect on how much we have benefited from our multicultural-ism and the enormous contribution that Canadians of all ethnic and religious backgrounds have made to the building of this great country.

subtopic: SENATE DELAY IN PASSING AMENDING BILL
SENATE DELAY IN PASSING AMENDING BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning representatives of the Creators and Artists of Canada, a coalition of over 20 artistic and creative groups, came to Parliament Hill to pressure the Liberal Senate finally to pass Bill C-60, the amendments to the Copyright Act.

April 18, 1988
Among those present were Dan Hill, Pierre Berton, Pat Durr, Timothy Findlay, Paul Siren and others.
The Liberal Senate is delaying and threatening to block this Bill which received all-Party support in this House. The artistic community has waited 64 years for copyright reform. These are the actions of a Liberal Senate which has turned a blind eye to the aspirations of Canadian artists and creators.

Bill C-60 recognizes that artists must have a certain copyright income. The Senate knows that by acting this way, it is calling into question years of effort for copyright reform.

If the Liberals in the Senate sabotage this Bill the artistic community will hold the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Liberal Party of Canada responsible. The Senators should realize that Canadian artists deserve a fair deal.

subtopic: SITUATION IN TORONTO-FUNDING OF METRO YOUTH JOB CORPS
SITUATION IN TORONTO-FUNDING OF METRO YOUTH JOB CORPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ironically the booming economy of Metropolitan Toronto has created a strange contradiction. Federal funding for a program aimed at making productive citizens out of hard-core unemployed youth is being threatened by the low Metro unemployment rate.
The Metro Youth Job Corps was initiated to help young people 16 to 24 years of age who are unable to get or keep a job because of their poor attendance or punctuality, or attitude toward their work, their supervisors, or their co-workers.
Unfortunately, the lower the unemployment rate the less federal funding there is available to train these young people to find and hold jobs. The kinds of young persons assisted by the Job Corps program will always be a problem for themselves and for society unless we give them a helping hand. I hope the Government will re-examine its funding criteria for this program.

Mr. Speaker, since last week, I have received many letters and comments from constituents deploring our attitude to the Turks' problem. I myself was very disappointed to hear the new Minister
responsible for this issue say that she could do nothing for them when we all know in this House that she has the authority to intervene without breaking the law.
This attitude led me to re-evaluate our work as parliamentarians of whatever party on this issue and several others. Unfortunately, we find that in our discussions and our decisions, political or partisan considerations too often override the public interest, that narrow-minded politics outweigh ethics, etc. For the Turks and the 40,000 people awaiting a reply, I hope that we will be able to hear the suggestions of those who can act, make the necessary corrections and amendments to the Immigration Act quickly and without political fanaticism and thus restore our image with our fellow citizens. Especially on issues where humanitarian considerations come first, we must set aside partisanship and together try to find a solution to the problem at hand.

Mr. Speaker, National Citizenship Week, which we are celebrating this year from April 17 to April 23, is an important occasion for all Canadians. It is particularly important for our young people.
The concept of citizenship represents an ideal of how we see ourselves as a society. It is important that we pass on from generation to generation an understanding of what citizenship means, the benefits it bestows and the duties that good citizenship entails.
This week, in classrooms all across Canada, tens of thousands of young Canadians will be taking part in many projects designed to build that understanding. Teaching our young people about Canada and about the rights and responsibilities of citizenship is one of the best investments we can make in the future of this nation.

maintopic: LUMBER EXPORTS-EFFECT OF INTEREST RATES AND EXCHANGE RATE OF DOLLAR
LUMBER EXPORTS-EFFECT OF INTEREST RATES AND EXCHANGE RATE OF DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the actions or, should I say, inactions of the Government, are once again laying the grounds for further hardship for Canadian lumber producers and their workers who depend on the U.S. market.
April 18, 1988

The holding of Canadian interest rates at current high levels and the rising value of the Canadian dollar are jeopardizing the competitiveness of not only our lumber exports but all our exports.
A growing number of Canadians are convinced that the maintenance of high interest rates in Canada, coupled with the rising value of the Canadian dollar, constitute a deliberate government policy to appease U.S. interests and secure U.S. support for the trade agreement to which the Government has tied its political future.
I say again: whose side is the Government on? A cut in interest rates would not only assist the average consumer but would go a long way to safeguarding jobs in our resource industries.
The NDP once again calls upon the Government to cut interest rates by one per cent to two per cent. But is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) listening?

Mr. Speaker, banks defend increased service charges because they pay higher interest rates on accounts. However, when asked for facts, that often turns out to be a myth.
For example, one Canadian has written to me about his opening a small account and after one month finding that the service charges were three times the amount received in interest. To make it worse, there had been no cheques, no withdrawals, no deposits and, as far as he could see, no service.

subtopic: ACQUISITION OF NEW AIRCRAFT-ROLE OF FORMER OFFICIAL
ACQUISITION OF NEW AIRCRAFT-ROLE OF FORMER OFFICIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians will no doubt remember statements by the former Minister of Transport who said in the House that Mr. Ramsey Withers had not been involved with the Air Canada airbus transaction.
I have here a letter, dated December 22, 1987, signed by Mr. Ramsey Withers. It states:
Thank you for your letter of December 7, 1987, in which you expressed concern over Air Canada's reported fleet plans and offered to assist in assessing these plans.
In today's highly competitive airline environment I do not feel at liberty to disclose Air Canada's future plans, but I am able to say that the article upon which your concerns are based was inaccurate in some significant areas.
Your very extensive experience and knowledge in the field of airline fleet
planning are well recognized in the industry . ..
Clearly there is contradiction here between statements by the Minister and the facts.

subtopic: CONSEQUENCES OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S POLICY
CONSEQUENCES OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY'S POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to talk about the New Democratic Party's position on defence in the light of recent changes towards an irrealistic policy.
As it stands today, the NDP policy calls for a withdrawal of our Canadian troops stationed in Europe, the cancellation of the NORAD agreement and pulling out NATO.
Our withdrawal from NATO will alienate our allies, not to mention the fact that we would be barred from the negotiation table which recently made it possible to conclude the FNI agreement.
Any change to NORAD would also involve huge expenditures for Canadians. For example, under the existing agreement our contribution amounts to only 12 per cent of the $7 billion being spent to modernize it. To that we can add annual operating costs of more than $100 million.
In short, Mr. Speaker, if Canada were to put an end to these alliances, as advocated by the NDP, it will cost every taxpayer more to have a less effective defence system in this country.

Mr. Speaker, this morning my Leader and I had the great honour of speaking with a woman of uncommon determination, eloquence and conviction, Dr. Helen Caldicott. The driving force behind the Nobel Prize winning Physicians for Social Responsibility and the founder of Women's Action for Nuclear Disarmament, Dr. Caldicott has devoted herself to preventing what she has aptly described as the "final epidemic", a nuclear holocaust.
Travelling the world simply with a suitcase and a vision, Dr. Caldicott has mobilized hundreds of thousands of men and women in her great crusade to end the nuclear arms race. Her message is one that we and millions of Canadians share, that national and international security can only be achieved

April 18, 1988
through disarmament and peace, that we can make Canada a nuclear weapons free zone, that we can end the militarization of the Canadian economy and that we can reverse Canada's increasing complicity in the world-wide trade in arms.
I urge Canadians to meet Dr. Caldicott as she continues her Canada-wide tour this week.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT EFFORTS TO REDUCE INTERNATIONAL OBSTACLES
GOVERNMENT EFFORTS TO REDUCE INTERNATIONAL OBSTACLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this past weekend an important meeting was held in beautiful British Columbia, bringing together representatives for 70 per cent of the world's international trade. The focus of discussion was barriers to trade and how to reduce them.
Unlike the opposition Parties in this house which state a desire to tear up current trade agreements, the federal Government continues to seek new and better ways of reducing these obstacles to trade.
Canada is a trading nation. Our national economic health is directly dependent on healthy foreign markets for our goods and services. The opposition Parties continue to demonstrate a total lack of understanding that our sovereignty, our culture and, indeed, our national social programs are only sustained by a strong healthy economy.
This Government believes in negotiation, consultation, conciliation, and discussion. We support GATT. We continue to initiate important new measures in GATT. Unlike the opposition Parties that want to ignore or reject GATT when an unfavourable decision for Canada is reached, we believe that the mandate and authority of GATT must be strengthened, as must our access to that vital U.S. market to the south. The Canadian public is developing this understanding. What a pity that the thinking of the Opposition is still mired in the 19th century.

subtopic: MINISTER'S ATTENDANCE AT CELEBRATION SPONSORED BY SIKH ORGANIZATIONS
MINISTER'S ATTENDANCE AT CELEBRATION SPONSORED BY SIKH ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the new Minister for Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) gave Canadians a fine demonstration of Cabinet solidarity over the weekend. The Minister attended a Baisakh celebration in Toronto planned by various Sikh organizations,
including those whose meetings the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) asked Canadian Premiers and other politicians by letter earlier this year to boycott. When the Minister was asked to explain why she attended the meeting in spite of her senior colleague's proscription, she had "no comment" on the contradiction.
I support the Minister's decision to attend the Basakhi celebration and to assure the Sikhs gathered there that the Government's aim is to achieve a better understanding with them. But surely it is time the Secretary of State for External Affairs recognized his mistake and recalled or renounced the advice he handed out so freely. Canadian politicians generally know their communities and can be trusted not to support activities that are illegal or destructive of other states. Let us have a proper regard by our Government for organizations in our communities which are working to advance human rights and the good of their own community.

Mr. Speaker, this past weekend we once again witnessed a new interpretation of the New Democratic Party position on defence as a result of its latest policy or, should I say, politics conference. In an attempt to obfuscate an already unintelligible policy on NATO and NORAD, the "No Defence Party" or NDP has taken a major step back from its long-standing position to withdraw from NATO.
This new position is an incredible thing. It threatens to alienate our allies because it calls for an immediate withdrawal of our troops in Germany thereby affecting the balance of power in Europe. It threatens to alienate the NDP's core supporters because it has consistently insisted on an immediate withdrawal from NATO and cancellation of the NORAD agreement.
Finally, it threatens to alienate all Canadians from the New Democratic Party because of what can only be perceived as an immature, irresponsible, and downright reprehensible act.
The Progressive Conservative Party has the only clear position on defence. Ours is the only Government willing to back up that position with realistic commitments. Finally, on the subject of platforms and positions, I would simply like to ask who is the spokesman on this subject. Is it Derek Blackburn, the NDP defence critic? Is it Bob White and the Seven Dwarfs, the NDP's leader in waiting? Or is the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) who so adamantly opposes this new position?
April 18, 1988

PROPAGATION OF THE FAITH IN CHURCHES

maintopic: PROPAGATION OF THE FAITH IN CHURCHES
subtopic: THE DEEDS OF TRINITARIAN ARMAND GAGNE-TRIBUTE TO VOLUNTEERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next Sunday at the Andre Laurendeau CEGEP in the beautiful riding of La Salle, a biennial event will take place that is extremely important, not just to the Montreal area but internationally. I am referring to the general meeting concerning the work of Father Armand Gagne, who is responsible for the propagation of the faith in the churches that heroically hold the torch of Christianity in countries behind the Iron Curtain.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore have the pleasure and the privilege to invite Members of this House to pay a well-deserved tribute to one hundred volunteers and about 3,000 general participants who will ensure that adequate funds are sent to Rome, to this Trinitarian Father from Ville-Emard, whose mission is to tell people that democracy still exists in our troubled world and to send this message to a civilization deprived of the most elementary freedoms, including the free expression of one's religious convictions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know that Hon. Members would want me to interrupt proceedings briefly to hear from the Deputy Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government, and I am sure all Members of the House, I wish to extend my sincere condolences to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) on the passing of his mother, Mrs. Phyllis Ross. Our prayers are with her and all members of the family.
Mrs. Ross led a full and vigorous life, a life of service to her country, to the Province of British Columbia, and to her family. She inspired more of the same with her son and her daughter, Brenda Norris.
On behalf of us all, Mr. Speaker, allow me to extend our deepest sympathies to the right hon. gentleman at this time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you can understand, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) is not in the House today. On his behalf I am very pleased to receive the words of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski). I will convey those words to the Leader of the Opposition.
Oral Questions
I also wish to say on my own behalf and on behalf of my colleagues that we want to express our deepest sympathy to the Leader of the Opposition and to his sister Brenda Norris on the loss of their mother. She was a very distinguished woman, an example well before her time of what women can accomplish in our society and how they can serve the entire country.
She became in her time the most senior woman in the Canadian Public Service. She went on to become the first woman chancellor of a university in the British Commonwealth. She accomplished this by virtue of the strength of her mind and her personality, being an example of a person standing alone, and raising a family alone, in a way that inspired her children with her example of service and intelligence.
The Bible, in the Book of Proverbs, speaks of a woman of valour. Truly, the mother of the Leader of the Opposition exemplified that concept to the utmost. Therefore, on my own behalf and on behalf of all of the colleagues of the Leader of the Opposition, we wish to extend to him and to his family our deepest sympathy on his tragic loss.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) and the House Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Gray) in extending to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) the deepest sympathy of the members of the New Democratic Party on the passing of his mother earlier today.
As has been noted, Mrs. Ross was an outstanding Canadian. In addition to having a distinguished son she established very much a reputation in her own right many years ago in this city as one of the forerunners, if I can put it this way, in the women's movement, achieving outstanding success in the Public Service of Canada. She also made a distinguished contribution to the Province of British Columbia.
We extend to the Leader of the Opposition our heartfelt sympathy on the passing of this woman who played such an important role in his life and, of course, extend those sympathies to his sister Brenda.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: CANADA-FRANCE DISPUTE-HARASSMENT OF CANADIAN AIR TRAVELLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In good part as a result of the fisheries dispute, we have seen an unprecedented deterioration of the relationship between Canada and France over the weekend leading to the recall of the French Ambassador.

April 18, 1988
Oral Questions
Canadians have been dismayed to see some of their fellow citizens harassed at French airports, with some of them having their passports confiscated. We understand that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has filed a protest with the French. However, some of the people who are now visiting France, or who are planning to do so shortly, would like to know more.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State whether he can provide an update report as to the situation at entry points to France. Can Canadians expect to be able to leave or enter France in a civilized manner without being harassed, or has the Government come to think that it will have to issue a travel advisory?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CANADA-FRANCE DISPUTE-HARASSMENT OF CANADIAN AIR TRAVELLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this incident of course arises directly from a long-standing negotiation regarding fisheries matters between Canada and France. This most recent and isolated episode was created by a decision by some French citizens from St. Pierre and Miquelon to take actions which challenged the law of Canada. When they challenge the law of Canada they are subject to the penalties of the law of Canada. That is what occurred in this case.
There was also an action authorized in France that involved delays imposed upon Canadians who were visiting in France. I protested those delays. We have been advised today that senior authorities in France have ordered that those delays be stopped.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada no longer has an Ambassador to France and France has recalled its Ambassador. The sad fact is that the two countries are not able to talk to each other in a normal fashion through Ambassadors, all of this at a time when there are differences between the two countries that the Government has not resolved and which have to be resolved quickly.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Deputy Prime Minister to explain to the House and to the country how the Government could let the relationship between Canada and France fall to this all-time low. What does the Government intend to do to normalize relations between our two countries? What has former Ambassador, Lucien Bouchard, been doing in Paris over the last three years?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not to take the whole day, among the things that former Ambassador Lucien Bouchard had been doing in Paris was to be very instrumental in achieving an agreement on the basis for establishing the international conference of la francophonie, an accomplishment which was impossible for years when the Government of this country was led by a Liberal Party of which the Hon. Member was a participant and supporter.
Among other matters that Mr. Bouchard was able to move forward was a quite dramatic improvement in the relations, whether in economic exchanges, science and technology, or in others.
In a third area it was possible for us, during the time that Ambassador Bouchard represented Canada in France, to begin to make progress on a very serious fisheries dispute that had been caused in part by a bad decision taken by a former Liberal Government with regard to the fisheries questions. Those are some of the things that have been done by Mr. Bouchard, since his name has been raised.
The Hon. Member is wrong on a couple of other points. He suggests that there is not full diplomatic interchange between Canada and France. That is false. There is that type of interchange between our two countries.
Third, there is scheduled, as there has been for some time, a meeting for Thursday of this week at which the negotiators of the two countries will come together again to see if we can make further progress toward resolving the fisheries dispute by resolution. We are hopeful that we might find some progress in that regard.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should say that our relations with France are very important to us as they are to France. We do not intend to allow those important relations to be diverted by an episode of a voyage by a few people from St. Pierre and Miquelon who were almost certainly seeking political profile.

subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF MARKETS WITH FRANCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF MARKETS WITH FRANCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State may be proud of Mr. Bouchard's achievements as our ambassador and of our relations with France, but the fact is, our relations have never been this tense. We don't even have a Canadian ambassador in Paris, and now France has recalled its own ambassador for consultation.
Canadians are being harassed at French airports. Passports have been confiscated, and Canadians certainly have every right to wonder what former ambassador Lucien Bouchard has been doing with his time in France during the last three years. Meanwhile, it's business as usual between Canada and France.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State or the Deputy Prime Minister whether they do not think the time has come to reconsider the suitability of continuing negotiations with France on major purchase contracts, including the purchase of a fleet of Airbus aircraft and those silly nuclear submarines. Is it going to be business as usual for the Government?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): There are two or three points I would like to make, Mr. Speaker. First of all, the Hon. Member certainly has a short memory, if he thinks relations between France and
April 18, 1988

Canada have reached a new low. I remember the statements made by General de Gaulle, and I remember the problems that arose between Canada and France. By contrast, the present situation is just a straightforward disagreement about a matter that is important to both countries. The way to resolve this disagreement is to continue negotiations on the fishing zone, and the next meeting has been set for Thursday. Canada intends to have its negotiators at the meeting to protect Canadian interests in the fishing zone. And as a Government that wishes to do business with everyone, we intend to continue to seek out opportunities for investment and projects involving Canada and France. Relations between our two countries have improved a great deal since the Mulroney Government came to power. We would like the situation to continue. We want to continue to take advantage of the possibility such a situation creates for this country.

subtopic: ARREST OF FRENCH NATIONALS-SUNDAY COURT HEARING
ARREST OF FRENCH NATIONALS-SUNDAY COURT HEARING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday after being taunted for over 12 hours the Government finally took a long overdue step, however symbolic, and arrested those persons who were aboard a vessel owned by the Government of France, for violating Canadian fishing regulations.
By what precedent did the Government of Canada agree to have a court hearing on Sunday, when it was scheduled for Monday, to allow for the early release of those people who had broken Canadian law, and to allow the Royal Bank of Canada to bail them out to the tune of over half a million dollars? By whose suggestion did the court sit on Sunday?

Sunday night wasn't-was God the Government of Canada? [English]

Mr. Speaker, would the Minister not agree that Canada is the country that is in a position of strength in this dispute? Can he guarantee Canadians that in the negotiations that are coming up on Thursday, the Canadian Government will go no further than a 12-mile zone around St. Pierre and Miquelon, and that the Government of France and the French metropolitan fleet from France will be treated the same way as anyone else who breaks Canadian law in Canadian waters? Can he guarantee that there will be no special Sunday soirees in court, let alone any special Sunday banking privileges?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the negotiations that will be proceeding again next Thursday, these are not negotiations to deal with the territorial boundary between St. Pierre and Miquelon and Canada. Those are matters that we have been trying now for several years to get before an international tribunal so that an international tribunal could decide that issue.
I can assure the hon. gentleman that Canada takes the position that France should certainly not have any territorial boundaries around St. Pierre and Miquelon that exceed 12 miles, if indeed it should even be 12 miles, and not something like the 200-mile economic zone it is claiming. However, that question is not now up for negotiation. We are trying to persuade France to agree with us to send that matter to an international tribunal for decision.
With respect to the French metropolitan fleet, I believe the events of the last several days have shown what action the Government takes without fanfare, without histrionics, and without hysteria, when foreign fleets or vessels fish in Canadian waters without a permit.

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO APPOINT LUCIEN BOUCHARD TO CABINET
OPPORTUNITY TO APPOINT LUCIEN BOUCHARD TO CABINET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Prime Minister decided to appoint Mr. Bouchard to Cabinet at the very moment of the most serious conflict between our two countries. Before this decision, did the Prime Minister discuss it with the Secretary of State for External Affairs and does the Minister agree with this decision?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, it is often difficult to know where to draw the line between ministerial and other conversations. But 1 can tell the leader of the New Democratic Party that I was one of Lucien Bouchard's present colleagues who suggested that he seek a position as a Minister in our government. I have great respect for his abilities and his vision of Canada. I am sure that he will continue to be an effective Minister in our Government. Of course, I was involved in the discussions that

April 18, 1988
Oral Questions
resulted in Mr. Bouchard's appointment to Cabinet. I think that it is important to know that the decision made by some French citizens from Saint-Pierre and Miquelon came after Mr. Bouchard's appointment to Cabinet. Our diplomatic relations with France are as strong as before. Mr. Bouchard's successor as Ambassador to France will be appointed shortly.

subtopic: TIMING OF AMBASSADOR'S APPOINTMENT AS MINISTER
TIMING OF AMBASSADOR'S APPOINTMENT AS MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question, of course, has absolutely nothing to do with Mr. Bouchard's personal competence. I certainly have no question about that or his past performance as Ambassador to France. The question is directly pertinent to the competence of the Government.
Since this crisis did not just begin before the weekend and has been ongoing for a number of weeks, was it not very irresponsible of the Prime Minister to take our Ambassador out of France and have him selected to go into a Cabinet, to run in a by-election that has not been called, in a part of Quebec that has not yet been selected, during the period of the most serious crisis in modern history between France and Canada? Was the timing not entirely wrong? That is the question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TIMING OF AMBASSADOR'S APPOINTMENT AS MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I learned over the weekend that the New Democratic Party has a very peculiar view of Canada's defence requirements and how we deal with them, but I did not know that they were also so confused about diplomatic practice. The Hon. Member is talking about a fisheries dispute that has been going on for 18 months, a fisheries dispute that we want to have resolved, a fisheries dispute in which negotiations are being carried forward by a very distinguished negotiator, Mr. Yves Fortier.
It is always the case that, when a diplomat leaves a post that is an important post in its relations with Canada, some files continue to be open. The Hon. Member laughs. He laughs, betraying his ignorance of the way diplomatic practices proceed.
The point I am making is that we cannot expect every Ambassador in the real world to stay in place until every important file which is current between another country and Canada is completed. That would be an absurdity. That would be a diplomatic practice as absurd as it would be to have a defence policy that said: "Well, we're going to pull out of NATO but we might not do it now. We just want you to know that for the first four years we might be there you couldn't trust us with a single secret, you couldn't trust us with a single plan of common action".

subtopic: TIMING OF AMBASSADOR'S APPOINTMENT AS MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has exceeded his capacity to go to the lowest level of argumentation. I did not think he could do it, but he did it today.
Now would the Minister deal with the issue? Since the Minister, earlier in Question Period, correctly acknowledged that the relationship between our two countries is important and is at a very low level, and since no one in his right mind would ever contend that there are not some files open that continue when Ambassadors are changed, the question is surely still pertinent, and would he answer it? Is it appropriate for a Government to take an Ambassador who is doing a good job out of his job while an ongoing crisis is under way in order to run in a by-election that has not even been called? That is the issue.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let us have a little honesty here.
Good idea.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
