Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say something about Bill C-l 17, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. I particularly appreciate the opportunity to expand on some observations I made just before we rose for lunch. I was commenting on the speech given by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), a colleague from a northern Ontario riding. The Bill we are dealing with covers a great deal of territory in its way. It represents the legislative amendments required to implement quite a number of federal sales and excise taxes and excise duty changes. These are changes the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced at various times, for instance, in his Budget of February 18, 1987, and then again in his Budget of February 10, 1988.
There were some changes proposed in the June 18, 1987, White Paper on tax reform and other changes were made in the December 16, 1987 White Paper on tax reform. The changes proposed at those various times have all been gathered together in this Bill, which brings forward for approval by this House of Commons and by the other place changes in the excise tax, sales tax and excise duty.
I am speaking in support of the amendment of my colleague, the Hon. Member for the Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin), for a six-month hoist. It is a classic opposition proposal to send this Bill away for six months so that the Government can reconsider, the intention being to have the matter dropped. It is appropriate to propose such a motion on this particular Bill because of the regressive nature of sales and excise duty taxation and because of the gross unfairness these tax changes represent for Canadians in some regions of Canada as opposed to Canadians in other regions.
In speaking to the motion to hoist Bill C-l 17 for six months, I want to examine the particular proposals made and to demonstrate why they are wrong in principle, wrong in their economic effect on the people of Canada and wrong as part of the fiscal policy of the Canadian Government. I note that among the changes in Bill C-l 17 there is a proposal to increase the sales tax on paint and wallpaper products from 8 per cent to 12 per cent. That strikes me as a substantial increase. Those who like to play with numbers would say immediately that it is a 50 per cent increase in the rate of taxation because it has gone from 8 per cent to 12 per cent. One can think of the building boom going on in various parts of the country and the way in which people are involved in improving their various properties, and one can readily see the burden represented in this 50 per cent increase in the rate of taxation on these products.
The Minister of Finance has been involved time after time since he was first appointed as Minister of Finance in 1984 in loading down Canadian families and homeowners with more and more taxes. I note that Bill C-l 17 will authorize an increase in the federal sales tax on beer, spirits, wine and tobacco products from 15 per cent to 18 per cent. That is a fairly significant increase. That is a 20 per cent increase in the
Excise Tax Act
rate of taxation. This is an area of taxation that Government after Government has looked at as fair game.
Obviously, when we speak about taxes on alcoholic beverages and tobacco we are speaking about sin taxes. No doubt the products involved rarely serve the good health of the persons involved. We know tobacco is very detrimental to good health. But this particular loading on of more taxes in this area means the taxes are paid by everyone who consumes the products no matter what their incomes. Some people may think, in the pursuit of virtue and the construction of a moral society, that we ought to try to tax these products right out of existence. Those, of course, with larger incomes will still be able to enjoy these products without feeling anything like the burden put upon those with low incomes, those who barely manage, and there are those who indulge themselves all too frequently at the expense of their families, their wives and children. In those cases I do not overstate the harsh reality of what the Minister of Finance is doing in laying on another of those sin taxes. He is reducing the well-being of far too many of our citizens who are already in very serious circumstances.
In these two areas, the tax on products used to beautify our homes and the tax on products used by people who want to relax and have a little pleasure in life, the Minister of Finance has added to the burden that low and middle-income Canadians have to bear. There is no distinction in the amount of tax one has to pay because one is taxed on the quantity one buys. There is clearly a limit as to how much can be consumed no matter what one's income might be. It is all too tragically the case, particularly with alcoholic beverages and tobacco, that those who are the least able to afford it, may well end up being the excessive consumers of the product. Again, if the intention is to tax these products out of existence, there might be an argument for it. But if the consequence of that action is to reduce the food and the necessities of life of family members, surely it is to be regretted, at the very least, and provides some of the reason why hoisting this Bill for six months is quite appropriate.
However, it was not in those areas of regressive taxation on which I focused my own comments earlier today, although the Hon. Member for Algoma, in responding to my comments, expanded on the regressive features. It is in terms of regional unfairness that I want to make some additional observations. There are some other changes for which Bill C-l 17 provides. First, this Bill establishes a 10 per cent tax on telecommunications services such as telephone and telex, although it does not include any charge on local residential telephone lines. In the imposition of a 10 per cent tax on long-distance telephone charges we have a very good example about which I will elaborate. I notice that the Chairman of the House Committee on Finance, who is here, is shaking his head. Presumably he is shaking it at something else, although I expect that he might agree. After all, he is a Member for a Toronto area riding. He knows how his constituents can do business and carry on social activities in all kinds of ways in the Metro Toronto area without ever incurring a long-distance charge.

April 18, 1988
Excise Tax Act
It would be quite fascinating to know how the long-distance charges of the citizens of Toronto compare with the longdistance charges incurred by people in northern Ontario. Compared with the citizens of Thunder Bay, which is in my own constituency, the difference might not be all that great. However, there are a great many northern Ontarians who live outside the local calling area of a city. In those cases they face very high costs of carrying telephone communications. They have to do this for all types of reasons, whether it is to make an appointment at the doctor or to make a contact on a business matter using the yellow pages, which are such a delightful way of finding out where we can get products rather than burning gasoline. If one wants to do that in the community of Pass Lake, for example, in my constituency, which is only some 30 miles out, those are all long-distance charges. I have constituents there who routinely, although they have modest enough incomes, run up month by month long-distance bills of $100, $150 or $200 and more.
That is an excellent illustration of the situation that faces some Canadians by contrast with those who live in the City of Toronto from which the Minister of Finance himself comes. Persons there can make a diversity of calls. They can ask, inquire about practically any product on earth and do so without ever getting close to a long-distance call. They can enjoy all the marvels that life in Metro Toronto offers in the way of society, culture and so on without facing anything remotely like the type of costs that my constituents face.
That is a nice indication of why constituents of mine began writing and calling when they first spotted this 10 per cent tax. They wanted to know from where it came. They wanted to know who had done this to them. They, living even in the City of Thunder Bay-and I am thinking now of some of my older constituents with children who are grown and gone to work in Toronto, Winnipeg or wherever, far from the City of Thunder Bay, which, too, is all too often another feature of northern Ontario life-are being faced with a 10 per cent tax without any cap on it. That is the same level of taxation that someone would face if one lived anywhere in the City of Toronto. That is surely manifestly unfair.
What I want to spotlight in this matter particularly is that when the on finance committee considered this matter it suggested that there should be a cap on it. It was suggested that there should be a limit to the amount of this telecommunications tax that a person could pay. That was designed to ensure that those who live in circumstances such as my constituents in northern Ontario did not pay a tax that was immediately proportional to the number of long-distance calls they had to make.
The Minister of Finance refused to accept that recommendation. He refused to put a cap on this tax so that a person might have to pay $3 or whatever it happened to be. However, if one has the misfortune of making $100 in long-distance calls
then one must pay another $10 in tax. That is that. There is no way of avoiding it.
There is an element of inflation in the country. Surely putting this tax on long-distance calls and on telex services is to place a cost on the transmission of information in our society that is bound to be reflected in the inflation rate. The Minister of Finance, who encourages the Governor of the Bank of Canada to keep the inflation rate stable or even to cut it down to zero, is being shamelessly hypocritical when he lays on a 10 per cent tax on telecommunication services and refuses to put a cap on it. This allows some Canadians to face the type of disproportionate burden that I have been describing.
There are other taxes in this Bill which are equally unfair in their effect on Canadians in one area and another. I notice that the gasoline tax was increased for the fourth time. We have faced this tax time after time. The Minister of Finance sees an opportunity every time he has to do a financial statement or a Budget in the fact that Canadians use cars and trucks. Some Canadians, in particular northern Ontarians, depend on aircraft to get about. There is another case of the unfairness of things. There is one cent more per litre on gasoline, which is four and a half cents a gallon. The taxes pile up each time a cent is placed on a litre. The Minister of Finance is probably grateful, despite whatever some of his Tory colleagues may have thought earlier, that the country went metric. This way he can raise taxes by one cent per litre rather than by one cent per gallon.
I remember as a graduate student living in Toronto 20 years ago. I do not know how typical my life was that year. I expect there are a good many Torontonians who own cars, which I did not that particular year. The really impressive thing, if one spends any time in the City of Toronto, is that thanks to the public transit system it is possible to get around and to enjoy a marvellous life in Metro Toronto without ever having to use an automobile.
Against that my constituents may very well have to drive 20 or 30 miles to work every day. They will be forced to take longer trips if they want to take the family for any type of holiday outing since they will want to cover some distance. In northern Ontario the distances are extreme.
If one is involved in the basic resource industries, the tax rebates have been increased in order to offset this. However, for all of those who are not involved in the basic resource industries here is another addition to the cost of doing business. Here is another inflationary impact on our society.
The high costs are being run up in terms of the purchases of fuel that have to be made and the burden of taxation on my constituents in Thunder Bay-Nipigon and in other parts of northern Ontario by contrast to the happy lot of people in our largest cities with excellent systems of public transit in order to spare people the expense of using gasoline while we have to use so much of it, and this pays all these tax costs. Lord knows whether or not my constituents in northern Ontario are not helping to maintain the subway system in the City of Toronto.
April 18, 1988

This is the ultimate demonstration of how unfair the system of regressive taxation across the board with percentage increases in one item or another is for Canadians. It is for those reasons that I oppose this Bill so profoundly. It is one thing to have a tax system that is oriented toward the ability to pay. It has been a challenge to be consistent even in that principle in income taxation. We have seen how often the Minister of Finance has rejected calls to him to ensure that our income tax system on individuals and corporations was fairly applied to everyone. That system is rife with exceptions. That system is rife with favouritism. It is favouritism of the wealthy, the powerful and the large corporations.
A splendid example of this came last week when Robert Campeau, after his triumphs in purchasing Federated Department Stores, offered some thoughts on taxation and some musings on social philosophy. What were his thoughts? He was opposed to various features of the Canadian social system. He was not honest enough himself to remind people that he had been a glorious recipient, as was his company, Campeau Corporation, of one aspect of the Canadian social system, that is, favouritism for the powerful and the wealthy in being able to avoid paying income tax for years through the 1980s. He did not talk about that, suggesting that others are free-loaders when he himself is a splendid example of corporate free-loading in Canada. He then ran off to the U.S. to swashbuckle about down there.
If we had a system that was fair to the ability to pay, there would be the revenues to allow us to do away with all of these excise taxes, sales taxes, and excise duties which are loaded on to people without regard to how much they have in the way of resources, and without regard to how much their incomes may be. They are simply loaded on them, grinding the poor into the dirt while the rich get away scot-free.
There is more than enough reason to reject this Bill. There is every reason to give it the six months hoist and tell the Government to go back to the drawing board, start from scratch, do the job right and in the fair way that Canadian taxpayers have been wanting for years and years.

We heard the Member for Thunder Bay- Atikokan (Mr. Angus) rant and rave about tax changes without recognizing the fact that every one of these tax changes have been debated before. The ones with respect to telecommunications, cable, and television are all part of the White Paper on taxation and were debated in full with public hearings; 178 witnesses appeared before the committee that travelled the length of the country and made comments on those taxes. These taxes were not objected to in the minutes of that committee.
I would have thought with that degree of unanimity across the House dealing with these particular measures that this Member and that Party would have said: "Well, we have
Excise Tax Act
heard this before. There has been a good inquiry into it, and let us accept them".
I want to ask the Hon. Member if he bothered looking at the finance committee report on the White Paper. Did he bother looking at the evidence with respect to the telecommunications tax? Does the Hon. Member realize that, as far as long distance charges are concerned, the result of the CRTC order is to reduce the price on long distance charges by 30 per cent? The effect of the taxation at a 10 per cent level is that the reduction, instead of being 30 per cent, is only 20 per cent, as far as households are concerned. Did the Hon. Member look at these matters? Does he realize that with tax reform there is a massive and significant reduction in taxes that individuals pay? The result is that the burden has to be paid somewhere, and that burden has been placed on business as that tax affects business almost entirely and totally. It is a transfer from individual taxation to business taxation.

In his last words the Hon. Member and chairman of the finance committee of the House indicates something of the ignorance of northern Ontario and generally the remote northern riding situation that I have been suggesting is at the heart of the problem. The Hon. Member may think that long distance is chiefly a business charge. That is not the case in northern Ontario. It is not the case for elderly constituents who live in the City of Thunder Bay who cannot keep in touch with their children across the country without making long distance calls and running up significant charges.
The question is not what I have read. The question is what the chairman of the committee is conscious of and what he remembers. My notes indicate that the committee considered this matter of telecommunications charges and that it actually recommended that there be a cap on them, in some limited recognition of what I am arguing that people in remote ridings face very high costs, and that it is simply unfair to them. Perhaps the Hon. Member's constituents can get away with making a couple of long distance calls a year, so he thinks that it is entirely a business matter. Those in remote ridings for whom long distance calls are a very important reality should find their obligation to pay a tax severely limited. That is the type of thing that I would expect him to be saying. I would like him to recognize that the Minister of Finance refused to accept that advice.
If my notes are wrong and the committee did not recommend that then I have been badly briefed, as sometimes happens.

The Hon. Member does not appreciate the fact that his constituents, via a CRTC order, are receiving a 30 per cent reduction in telecommunications tax for long distance purposes. The effect of this tax imposed on his constituents is that instead of getting a 30 per cent reduction, they are only getting a 20 per cent reduction. Does the Hon. Member not realize that the burden is coming down? I was wondering if he

April 18, 1988
Excise Tax Act
wanted to tie those things together, because that has to happen.
As far as the far northern branches are concerned, I suspect that there are not any of the conditions in his constituency, although I may be wrong, that would have been affected by that particular recommendation the Hon. Member is talking about.

I apologize to the Hon. Member for not noting his CRTC reference as well. It is not necessarily to the Government's credit. It has been an ongoing process for the CRTC to consider how telephone costs should be borne, given the way in which the technology reduces the expenses of those transmissions. Here is a reduction, and this is how real progress occurs, when it is possible to reduce the cost of things significantly. The Minister of Finance, of course, sees the opportunity for a revenue grab to get part of that, so that Canadians do not get the full benefit of the progress, if it really is progress.
The other possibility in this rate rebalancing is to load down the residential telephone user, the person who rents the telephone, pays for the service on a monthly rate, with a significant increase in charges. There has been much concern to ensure that that does not happen in any excessive manner.
As far as reductions are concerned, we have seen the CRTC in an ongoing battle, in particular with Bell Canada, which does not want to carry through the reductions. It is going to other courts to try to turn a ruling back, and it will do its best to keep what it can. Certainly, there has been a saving there. Like all Canadians, I appreciate progress that produces economic gains for us.
If the Member is correct that the provision that I was alluding to, the $3 cap, would have done nothing for northern Ontario, that only underscores my indignation that the resident of Toronto may well be able to avoid paying any of this tax while leading a rich and well-rounded life, while some of my limited income constituents, many of them seniors living on pensions or in the situation of many senior women or widows who are living on the edge of poverty find themselves faced with a 10 per cent tax on the long distance charges they make to keep in touch with their children. That is why I am angry. I suspect that is an emotion that the chairman of the Commons finance committee probably would share, if he really thought about it and brought his mind into the situation of my constituents in Thunder Bay-Nipigon.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. The Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-17 on behalf of my Party and caucus. The purpose of this Bill is to implement the many sales and excise tax increases announced by the Conservative administration in the Budget of February 18, 1987, and June
18, 1987 and December 16, 1987 with respect to tax reform proposals, and recently the February 10, 1988 Budget.
One of the pertinent aspects within these fiscal plans and arrangements that irks Canadians and angers Members on this side of the House is essentially the commitments and promises made by the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) back in 1984.
They promised Canadians very clearly that the Tory administration had no desire to raise the taxes of Canadians. Yet following the September 1984 election, we in this House and Canadians across the country not only saw but experienced unprecedented tax increases.
I think it is worth recalling that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister promised not to raise taxes. On March 6, 1984, the Minister of Finance, as reported in Hansard, said:
We will reduce spending. We will refrain from increasing taxes, which are
already too high.
Not to be outdone by that promise, the Prime Minister, according to Le Devoir for November 29, 1984, said:
Canadians pay a good deal of money for government services and feel that
they are already paying quite enough.
Yet, despite those statements, we in this House have had to sit in our places, despite our urgings and complaints about what we hear from average Canadians when we meet with them in our constituency offices, when we visit them in their places of work or in their homes, and we have had to endure and witness a litany of tax increases which makes all the promises simply a sham. But it is more than that. These so-called promises have instituted a certain kind of cynicism among Canadians about their elected representatives and political institutions.
Right after those statements were uttered in 1984, we had a sales tax increase from 9 per cent to 10 per cent. In January,
1986	the sales tax went from 10 per cent to 11 per cent. In April, 1986 there was another increase from 11 per cent to 12 per cent. Those three increases have had an impact of raising tax revenues to the tune of $3 billion, taken from the pockets of Canadians. The Government between the years of 1985 and
1987	extended the sales tax on candy, soft drinks, fast food and snacks. In January 1988 there was a sales tax increase from 8 per cent to 12 per cent on paper, wallpaper and toys. In September, 1986 there was a gasoline tax increase of two cents a litre, and an additional one cent increase was imposed in January, 1987, with a further one cent increase on February 19, 1987. There were other increased taxes on alcohol and tobacco. The first one came in January, 1985. Since then there have been three increases.
Canadians accept their duties as citizens of this country. We enjoy a certain kind of lifestyle, we receive services and programs from our government and accept as part of this
April 18, 1988

contract with Canada the imposition of taxes so that we and our children and their children's children can live in a country as blessed as Canada is. Canadians are prepared to share the burden of taxes to maintain the social, economic, cultural and political stability that we enjoy as a nation. What is upsetting to Canadians is that they realistically perceive and realistically believe that some of us are being asked to share a disproportionate share of the national burden. They are correct.
When we look at the litany of tax increases we have had, we have to ask ourselves what is the cumulative impact on the average Canadian household. When you do that, you find there is an unfairness in the system. If you take the four federal budgets presented to this House by the Conservative Government, you will find that a Canadian earning $15,000 to $20,000 a year will by 1990 have to pay nearly a 36 per cent increase in taxes from the tax level of 1984. An individual earning between $35,000 and $45,000 will have to face an increase in his or her taxes of approximately 12 per cent. But those Canadians in the $100,000 bracket will have an increase of only 4 per cent. If you are fortunate enough to be in the circle of Canadians who earn $200,000 and up, your increase is only 2 per cent. That is the spectrum, Mr. Speaker.
On the one hand, a $15,000 wage earner has a 36 per cent tax increase while on the other hand a $200,000 wage earner has only a 2 per cent tax increase. You can say what you want and cut it in however technical financial language that you can, but at the end of the day Canadians are seeing that proportionate tax sharing as being fundamentally and irresponsibly unfair. It is having an impact.
We are seeing the squeeze play. Those who are working class Canadians and those who are middle-class Canadians or who think of themselves in those two categories are being squeezed. If you talk to Canadians in those economic brackets, you will hear that they are finding it more difficult with each passing day to maintain their current standard and status. If you talk to Canadians who see themselves as middle-class Canadians, they will tell you that they are finding it hard to stay in the middle class section.
Because of the cumulative effect of these fiscal policies by the Conservative Government people are seeing a stratification of class like never before. For the first time in many years, perhaps for the very first time, Canadians see themselves through various polling studies being more in a class stratification while the British see themselves in very well delineated classes by class designations. That is dangerous. One of the things about which we have pride is an underplaying of class stratification seen in other societies.
The taxes and budgets that we have had do not help. These taxes and budgets do not provide the bridge or shorten that gulf, that growing disparity, both in reality and in feeling which is dividing those who are falling more and more every day between the haves and the have-nots.
There is a struggle in certain communities and families at the end of the month. Canadians who face increased property
Excise Tax Act
taxes on their homes, coupled with increased federal income taxes, excise and sales taxes are having a tough time making ends meet. This struggle is all the more acute if you happen to be a senior and you want to hold onto the home that took a lifetime of work and sacrifice to build and own. If you are a single mother trying to keep the household together, these numbers make your life very difficult.
Individuals who are collecting workers' compensation because of injuries incurred on construction jobs face property taxes and increased sales taxes. We will meet those construction workers at some point in time in our constituency offices. They will be looking for help, looking for answers, looking for direction.
For a family with two parents, both of whom are working in middle-class jobs, with kids to clothe and send to school, the end of the month is not a day that is looked forward to. We in this House of Commons have to look beyond the numbers. We have to know that behind these numbers are real, living Canadians who have real, living struggles.
We in this House have recognized the need to try to pull Canada ahead, to leave it one step forward from where it was when we found it. We must recognize as well that as Canada goes forward, we cannot allow some Canadians to be left lagging behind. While we will not have a perfect system, we cannot have those who earn $200,000 per year paying an increase in taxes of 2 per cent while those who earn $15,000 per year are paying an increase in taxes of 36 per cent. That gulf must be minimized. We must bridge that difference so that Canadians in the lower income brackets can have the perception that though it will be difficult, they know that their next door neighbours are also pulling their weight and other Canadians in similar circumstances are paying for the future of their country.
What breeds contempt, anger and cynicism is having such a perverse difference in the rates based on the incomes brought in at the end of the year. That is why we complain. That is why we are not timid about standing in our places and talking about these issues. They need to be talked about.
The chairman of the finance committee has done a good job on the finance committee and he has been recognized for that. However, he asks why the Opposition is continuing to talk about this matter if it has already been analysed in committee and in the Budget. We are talking about it because there have been no changes. These voices of anger across the country have fallen on deaf ears. Canadians continue to have their struggles. That is why we are still talking about it. That is why we are still prepared to debate it. We are talking about two different visions of Canada, and Canadians ought to have the opportunity to witness these debates on their television sets and to agree with whatever vision they believe to be correct.
We will continue to argue for a tax system in which Canadians must participate that comes a step closer to being

April 18, 1988
Adjournment Motion
equitable and fair and to breeding the confidence that all Canadians are giving a bit and sacrificing a bit for the building of a great country. Everyone must shoulder the burden, pull up his or her shirt sleeves and put the shovel to the ground.
We do not want to go the way of Great Britain where there are great stratifications in classes, and everyone knows them. If we do not want to go in that direction, then we had better do something about it by changing these numbers. That is why we are standing up today and why we will continue to stand up.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill involves certain sales tax and excise tax items that have largely been debated before and are part of the over-all thrust of paying the bills of the country. These are not brand new propositions that have not been broached before or have not been subject to debate.
I wonder why we hear this haranguing about the problems of taxation. I appreciate that the taxes in Canada are too high, but so is the debt of Canada too high. That Hon. Member was responsible, as a member of the Liberal Party, for putting us where we are.
If we get into the glue, we have to do something about it. I wonder if the Hon. Member has any suggestions for what public expenditures he thinks ought to be cut, what pensions, for example, ought to be cut, in order that we would not have to levy the taxes set out in Bill C-117.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has asked me why we are haranguing the Government about what he calls old taxes. As I mentioned in my remarks only a few moments ago, we are debating these policies because we believe them to be wrong. We believe them to be fundamentally unfair. We find that they impose a greater degree of burden on many Canadians and their families who can least afford to pay.
The Hon. Member asks what I would suggest instead. I suggested that we cannot afford to have $200,000-per-year wage earners facing 2 per cent increases while $15,000-per-year wage earners are facing 36 per cent increases. My suggestion would be to minimize that difference. We would find that we would still bring in the capital required to fund our services and programs. Not only that, we would regain the confidence of many Canadians who will again believe in the fairness of the system.
We as a country have existed for a long, long time. We have not had to place such a high proportion of the taxes on the poor and middle-income earners. It is only in the last four years that we have seen a tax imposition that has been unprecedented. Unless the Government is prepared to make it fairer, I suggest that it remove itself from governing the country and allow the people who can do it properly and with some compassion as well to do it.

Mr. Speaker, on several occasions in the last week or two the Government has made appeals for the co-operation of members of the opposition Parties. Something occurred this morning and just now which means the Government is insincere and does not want that cooperation. It could not care less about Parliament and its traditions. After its demands, requests, wooing and handing out of sugar in an attempt to gain the co-operation of the opposition Parties, the Government then does a dumb thing like extending the hours.
I want to inform my hon. friends opposite that I am something of an expert on extended hours. In balmier days we kept the Government sitting until six o'clock and eight o'clock in the morning. Member and I would just like him to know that even when we start off the session in the morning Members do not necessarily have to be in their seats in order for us to have a quorum. I know how intelligent the Hon. Member is as far as the rules of this House are concerned, but I must say to him that it is not necessary for any Hon. Member to be in his seat as long as he is in the Chamber to a count of 21 Members.
I do not wish to get into an argument with my friend who I have known for many, many years. The Chair would just like to hear his speech, please.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I hope there are more than you who would like to hear my speech. You see, there they go again out the door. If they do not have duties somewhere else then they should be sitting in their place in the

April 18, 1988

House earning their keep. I hope I can find enough of them who have earned their keep.
Let us get back to the issue of federal sales and excise taxes. I was saying, before I was interrupted by my colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), who has done properly, that if the Government was living up to what it said, promised, and the way it acted in this Chamber in the years when the Grits were in power, we would not have this Bill in front of us now.
Now you and I, Mr. Speaker, had to suffer through listening to the Conservatives making the same speeches that the Liberals made about sales and excise taxes when the Liberals were in power. Now we have to suffer through listening to Liberals making the same speeches that Conservatives made in the terrible Liberal days about sales and excise taxes, which proves again that there is no difference between them except that one is in and one is out. They have the same basic economic philosophy. They may differ on a minor detail about how they are going to do it and who they are going to do it to, but there is no basic difference.
I can remember Conservative Members getting up in support of speeches by NDP Members and NDP Members getting up in support of Conservative speakers about the terrible situation concerning deferred corporation taxes. There is over $32 billion on the books of Canada, an interest-free loan which corporations will never pay which has been accumulating since the mid-1950s. If they were charged just the bank rate, which is the best interest rate that preferred borrowers can get, which last Thursday was 8.8 per cent, that would bring in $2.7 billion in interest on deferred corporation taxes.
By the way, if we were to start charging that you would be surprised at how fast they would start paying back their deferred corporation taxes. By doing that the Government could cut its required revenues from sales and excise taxes by over 50 per cent.
If we were to lower the interest rate by 1 per cent or, at worst, set it at no higher than the U.S. rate, the business community would be able to borrow more and would put more people to work. Those people would purchase a lot of things and the Government's revenues in income tax and a low sales tax would increase accordingly. It would have as much, or more, money as it says it needs in the current fiscal year. If we were to impose a modest minimum tax of 10 or 15 per cent on all corporations which show a profit, the 60,000 corporations which earned a profit last year and will pay nothing this year would pay a minimum tax. Tories have been known to put a minimum tax on the individual taxpayer. Why can the same rule not apply to corporations? Why the double standard?
Corporate profits to the end of October, 1987, were up by 26 per cent. Their tax bill went up by 15 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Again I do not see a quorum in the House. We seem to be having a lot of trouble this afternoon keeping the government Members in the House and they are the ones who want extended hours.	'

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I am going to need it. We are going to keep flushing these birds out of the bushes very frequently. The Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) has made it plain that they do not want our co-operation, so be prepared.
I was saying that corporate profits to the end of October, 1987, were up by 26 per cent and their taxes in total went up by 15 per cent. Therefore, they had 11 per cent to their benefit. That would be all right, but why did the same thing not happen for the individual taxpayer? Personal incomes stayed about the same. Most of them did not quite keep up with inflation, but let us say that they stayed about the same. Personal taxes went up by 16 per cent. The corporations get to take home an extra 11 per cent of increased profits after taxes but the individual taxpayer, the average family with two children earning about $30,000 a year, pays more.
The best economic brains on all sides of the political spectrum have said that a sales and excise tax is a regressive tax, that those on the lowest end of the income scale have to pay proportionately more than those on high incomes. I have always believed that that is what is so unfair about exemptions. If you raise the exemption of the person in the 50 per cent tax bracket by $1,000 he saves $500, but the person in the 16 per cent tax bracket, because of his low income, saves $160. That is unfair.
I want to remind the House that in the great debate of 1984 the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said twice in response to my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), who raised the whole matter of tax fairness in the
April 18, 1988

tax system: "You're right, Ed". Since we are right and the Prime Minister has said on national television that we are right about a fair tax system, why in the name of heaven are we dealing with a Bill such as this? It flies in the face of tax fairness. It flies in the face of equity. It flies in the face of teaching people decency. It shows an unmitigated bias for those who have and a terrible insensitivity for those who have not.
Surely the Government could go back to the drawing board on legislation such as this, or could ask for a new royal prerogative and make substantial amendments to this legislation so that it will be a beginning to a fair tax system. Canadians believe they are being unfairly treated because they see it happening to them every day. They will notice this particularly between now and the end of April while they are filling out their income tax returns.
I had the honour to visit Sudbury on Saturday. There will be an excellent New Democratic Party Member of Parliament from Sudbury, a United Church minister. I know that we will want to welcome Bill Majors as a new Member of Parliament here before too long. Another clergyman will not do any of us any harm.
In Sudbury last Saturday I spoke with small business people, professionals and steelworkers who are in the process of filling out their income tax returns. They know from filing their returns and knowing what others who are much richer than they are paying that they are being unfairly treated. Even the Prime Minister said that.
It is time the Government withdrew this Bill or rewrote it. If it introduces a fair system of taxation it will have the support of my Party. It can take all the credit it wants. The people of Canada deserve a fair tax system because it is long past due.
Mr. Speaker, there were many occasions when you and I demanded fairness for people in our constituencies and throughout the country but did not receive it from the Liberals. Now, we are not receiving fairness from the Conservatives.

Mr. Speaker, I wish nevertheless to deal briefly with this Bill which will impose a great many sales and excise tax increases which, contrary to what some people may think, have already been announced and for which we are already paying. I do not know what would have happened if the Government had been defeated or had called an election, for it would be collecting taxes which would not have been noted by the House.
But, for the information of our listeners these taxes are the result of the February 1987 Budget, Mr. Speaker, I insist on this, as well as from the tax reform of June 18, 1987-I emphasize 1987-of December 16, 1987, and the February 10, 1988 Budget.
Excise Tax Act
Of course, I could not forget this date of February 10, because it was on that date, 24 years ago, that I came here for the first time as the elected member for the Montreal-Saint-Denis riding, a riding which has undergone a great many changes, but which I would represent should the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) decide to call an election after July the 13th-I repeat, July the 13th. If he calls an election before, I hope to be a candidate for the present riding of Montreal-Saint-Denis.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that all these taxes to please the Government Whip, Mr. Fennell, who is giving me his undivided attention and whom I prefer to call by his name-in order to cooperate, I shall not read the whole list of these taxes. But the Canadian people are paying them even if they have not yet been voted by the House of Commons. These are hidden taxes, so people are not too sure who imposed them, but these are major taxes, Mr. Speaker. A 12 per cent tax on snack foods and they said: Children are being taxed, but they forgot to tax rich people! In 1987-88 it will produce $60 million in revenues and, according to the 1988-89 estimates, that will rise to $80 million. A 4 per cent increase in the cigarette and tobacco tax. I take this opportunity to say that I have not smoked since this morning and I find it very difficult. . .
Hear, hear.

I know, it is a very bad habit, and I say that to the people who are listening to me. Smoking is a very bad habit and I hope to speak long enough not to smoke this afternoon. At least I will try not to smoke until tonight.
This tax was imposed on February 19, 1987 and brought in $70 million last year and it will again bring in $70 million this year. A $4 increase in the tax on every airline ticket was imposed on May 1 and August 1, 1987. The higher gasoline tax which became effective on April 1, 1987 yielded $30 million this year.
There was also another major increase which is not always immediately obvious and which came on stream as a result of the tax reform of June and December 1987, a 10 per cent tax on long distance telephone calls, along with another one of 8 to 10 per cent on cable TV. Both together will bring in $870 million in 1988-89, and estimates range from $945 million in 1989-90 to $1 billion in 1990-91.
There are other tax increases-my colleague mentioned them- on paint and wallpaper, and the sales and excise taxes must be remitted more often, another $1.6 billion. As people used to say in my neighbourhood, that is not chicken feed! A total of $1.6 billion. A record 15 to 18 per cent tax increase on alcohol and tobacco. I insist that smoking is a bad, a very bad habit. I am addicted to it, I shake it, I am hooked again. I have not indulged since this morning, and it is now 4.30 p.m., but anyway that tax will bring $175 million this year, Mr. Speaker, $175 million next year, and another $175 million the year after.

April 18, 1988
Excise Tax Act
We now come to the February 1988 Budget. Another lc. per litre increase on the excise tax on gas. That adds up to 4.5c. a gallon. On April 1st, 1988, it went unnoticed, but it was not an April fool's hoax-$225 million were suddenly imposed that day on unsuspecting taxpayers. That hidden tax will bring $300 million next year, Mr. Speaker, and another $300 million the year after.
That coming from a Government that suggested we were paying too much in taxes. I am realistic enough to realize that any expenditure must be taxed. But they should stop stating they will not impose new taxes during election times, because three and a half years later, we now find this is the Government that taxed the most after saying it would not tax that much, and that was a public commitment, a commitment that was taken at face value by the people who voted to change the Government and who found themselves in a situation that is much worse than before.

We have an old expression which comes from my grandfather: "Tory times are hard times".

I feel this is increasingly accurate. The Minister of Finance suggested he would cut spending he would not raise taxes which, according to what he said, and I was here in this House, Mr. Speaker, I was in Parliament when the Minister of Finance on March 6, 1984, not any Minister of Finance but the current one, one of the two Ministers from Toronto ... At least in Toronto they are lucky, they have two. In Montreal I wonder if we have one or half of one. The two largest Canadian cities are underrepresented in Cabinet, even though everything may not have been perfect before. But when we look at the then impressive delegation from Montreal in Cabinet, we knew that the interests of Montreal were protected. Presumably this Government decided to erase Toronto and Montreal from the election map. This seems clear to me.
But again it is the same Minister of Finance who on March 6, 1984, stated they would not raise taxes because tax levels in Canada were already too high. And as usual I cannot but call him my excellent friend-what else could I call him?

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was quoted in le Devoir in November of 1984, after the election, as saying: "It's been done before me. I am going to do it too".

"Canadians pay a whole lot of money for Government services. They feel they are paying enough". Well, what happened since November 29-that is the day before my birthday, this is why I recall perfectly those dates-there has been-it is unbelievable, I see my colleague who is smiling, and I am also smiling because the poor Prime Minister is always caught up in his
rhetoric. How do we reconcile today's actions with yesterday's promises? That is what's happening.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a quick look at the revenue. I don't want to keep on talking just to play a trick on the Chair. If other speakers come forward, we might still be here tonight. In any case, let's look at the revenue.
In 1984-85, individual income taxes amounted to $29 billion; in 1988-89, to $45.4 billion. That was from people who paid enough income tax, according to Le Devoir of November 29, 1984. It was from people who paid too much income tax, the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said on March 6, 1984. I repeat: individual income taxes amounted to $29.3 billion in 1984-85 and $45.4 billion in 1988-89. Corporations were a lot better off: they paid only $9.4 billion in 1984-85 and $12 billion in 1988-89. In 1984-1985, excise and sales taxes went from $13.7 to $24.3 billion. Other taxes worth $18 billion increased to $21 billion in 1984-85 for a grand total, in that same year, of $70.9 billion if my researchers' figures are correct and I believe they are. That became $103.3 billion in 1988-89.
And that from a Government who said, on March 6, 1984, that they would not increase taxes that Mr. Wilson found too high already. The Right Hon. Prime Minister (M. Mulroney) also said in Le Devoir on November 29, after the election, that taxpayers were paying through the nose for Government services and felt like they were paying too much. Well, Mr. Speaker, they have paid a lot more since then.
Once more, I must point out that this Government broke its promises and collected hundreds of millions, even billions of dollars more in taxes. And there lies the danger, Mr. Speaker, as I try to convince my own party to quantify its promises. We are currently developing our electoral platform. People are becoming cynical about politics. They do not often believe politicians because they listen to electoral campaign speeches. Candidates promise this and that and, two or three years later, they take the opposite course of action.

I am not surprised that people are becoming more and more cynical because they believed passionately during the election campaign that here was a Party which would be the kind of Party they wanted, and so it was elected. But it was promises, promises, promises. Then they turn around and they see that all the promises were broken. I am not at all surprised that people become very cynical when they talk about politics.
I am suggesting to my own Party that we put a price on every promise that we are going to make in the next election. We are at the moment writing our electoral platform. It is not an easy task.

It is not an easy thing because we well know that to win votes, we have to make promises left and right, promises in the
April 18, 1988

Atlantic, the Far North, Montreal, Toronto, the West. But we must still have a sense of responsibility. So Mr. Speaker, I hope that the party I represent will have a sense of responsibility the next time and will quantify the expenditures that we will have to impose on the people as a result of our promises or our election platform and that we will stop lying to the people by making completely unacceptable promises because we know in advance, when we make them, that we cannot pay for them. So we will have to tax. And that has happened to the tune of billions and billions of dollars. That is why we took the time required. That is why I wanted to stand in my place this Monday afternoon, April 18, and tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the more I read these promises, this pile of promises, the more I see the increasing numbers of people telling me that almost all this government's promises have been broken. I just wanted to point out some of them. And by speaking out, I hope to help political parties a little to act more wisely in the coming elections that may be held next year.

I see that you are ready to jump with the motion, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if I should not keep talking.
No.

There is only one person who can tell me to sit down here. It is Your Honour and certainly not the third Party which will be the fourth Party after the next election.
Having said all that, I will still show some co-operation and allow members of that Party to hearken to what I have just said. One thing is for sure, and at least members of the New Democratic Party will agree with me when I say it. It is that Tory times are hard times. That is what my grandfather said. That is what my father said. That is what I will say.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SENIOR CITIZENS' DAY DESIGNATION OF NATIONAL DAY
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General be empowered to study the question of designating, as National Senior Citizens' Day, the second Sunday in June each year in order to recognize the outstanding contribution made by senior citizens to Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today in support of a motion which would recognize the outstanding contributions of senior citizens in Canada. My motion, which I hope will receive the support of Members on all sides of the House, reads as follows:
That the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General be empowered to study the question of designating, as National Senior Citizens' Day, the second Sunday in June each year in order to recognize the outstanding contribution made by senior citizens to Canada.
This motion was appropriately seconded by my hon. colleague and friend from Beaches who has done an outstanding job over the years speaking on behalf of the New Democratic Party as our official spokesperson on senior citizens' issues. I intend to concentrate, during the few minutes available to me, on some of the concerns of the senior citizens of Canada in the areas of health care, community support and services, housing and pensions.
I might just say that this is an issue which I have been interested in from the very earliest age. Indeed, the first volunteer job I had was at the Napier Personal Care Home where I worked as a volunteer with senior citizens, helping them do their shopping and calling bingo. I did this at the age of 16 years, so I got involved at an early age with volunteer work with seniors.
Later, I had the honour of serving as a member of the board of directors of the New Vista Society in Burnaby, B.C.'s largest seniors' housing complex. The New Vista Society was

April 18, 1988
National Senior Citizens' Day
founded by a great pioneer of the CCF, Ernie Winch, who did an incredible job in service to seniors and indeed to the people of Burnaby for many, many years as the CCF MLA for Burnaby.
As well, it is appropriate that I note the extraordinary contribution made by leaders of the CCF and the NDP at the national level who have acted as tireless advocates for the rights of seniors in Canada. M. J. Coldwell and J. S. Woods-worth single-handedly pressured the Liberal Government of the day into implementing old age pensions. Yes, the people were means-tested at the age of 70, but certainly it was M. J. Coldwell and J. S. Woodsworth, those great CCF leaders, who established that fundamental principle.
Then, of course, there is the indefatigable Stanley Knowles who served for so many years as a Member of this House with such great distinction, over and over again speaking out for seniors, for better pensions and for dignity for those who have served our community over the years. Of course, it is particularly appropriate in the context of health care to mention Tommy Douglas, who in fact represented the constituency that I have the honour of representing now, Burnaby-Seymour. Certainly we join today in paying tribute to people such as Ernie Winch, M. J. Coldwell, J. S. Woodsworth, Tommy Douglas and indeed, my own colleague, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), who has done such an outstanding job in this area.
I am not today speaking solely of the role of the Government of Canada in improving the lot of seniors and in recognizing the contribution made by seniors. I also want to highlight one particular area of concern for immigrants from the United Kingdom who are now entitled to a pension from the United Kingdom. However, the Conservative Thatcher Government of the United Kingdom has refused to pass on the cost of living increases to which they are entitled. Certainly justice demands that these senior citizens originally from the United Kingdom receive the increases to which they are entitled.
It is true that the Government has taken an important first step in recognizing the contribution of senior citizens, recognizing the contribution of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) by appointing him as Minister of State for Senior Citizens. I am speaking, of course, of a Member of Parliament who is admired, respected and loved on all sides of the House, and I speak of the Hon. Member for Northumberland who has done such an outstanding job in this important capacity.
This motion is important both in terms of symbolism and of action. Just as we recognize each year the contribution of our mothers on Mother's Day and of our fathers on Father's Day, so too I suggest it is appropriate to recognize the contribution made by senior citizens in Canada.
I mentioned some particular concerns of senior citizens and I would like to touch on some of them now. One of the major concerns is health care. Older people, of course, are some of the most frequent users of the health care system, in terms of both acute and chronic health problems. We recognize a need
in Canada to study the important and emerging area of gerontology. This is an area of study for health care and social agency professionals. This recognition should be made by promoting gerontology as a field of study for the future and by way of increased funding by the federal Government for universities and research agencies in the field of gerontology.
Another area of major concern for senior citizens in my constituency of Burnaby and indeed those throughout the country is the question of affordable and accessible health care. Affordable health care is absolutely vital to seniors who remain on fixed incomes. Certainly we have concerns that the recent legislation covering the generic drug industry may in fact result in a significant increase in the price of essential drugs in the future. These are concerns that must be addressed by the Government.
As well, one of the most devastating concerns for seniors is the question of isolation, of loneliness. It has been said many times that friends are good for your health, and when it comes to seniors, nothing could be more accurate. In my riding, for example, which I have had the honour of representing for almost nine years now, there are over 74 different senior citizens' groups.
With respect to community support, once again I would like to use the example of my own riding because we are fortunate in having not only a large number of senior citizens, who live both at home and in senior citizens' facilities, but they are also very active. They work with their peers in providing many needed services in the community. After all, it is the community where services are needed. I am proud to be a member of a community which is prepared to look at the challenges posed by its large number of seniors.
For example, we have the Burnaby United Way Services for Seniors group ably chaired by Eddy Fisher which brings together a number of different services for seniors in order to provide the most efficient and needed services in the community. As well, we have the Seniors Bureau of New Westminster, presided over by an exceptional woman, Corol Strand-berg, the executive director. It provides a wide range of services to seniors in the Burnaby-New Westminster area. These include shopping, friendly visiting outings, income tax clinics and handyman service. Most of those services are provided on a voluntary basis. I suggest this could serve as a model for other communities in realizing that seniors want to remain independent and active when well past retirement.
The municipality of Burnaby provides a number of important resources to my constituents, whether it be the Cameron Rec Centre, Bonsor Recreation Centre, Confederation Centre, or the Edmonds Community Centre for the Retired which provides special programs, events, workshops and bus trips for Burnaby senior citizens.
I mentioned that in my constituency there is a particularly significant number of seniors. Many of them live in seniors'
April 18, 1988

housing complexes, including the New Horizons Facility, Seton Villa in North Burnaby, the Salish Tower, Doug Drummond Manor, Hall Towers, and many other outstanding facilities. In March, the mayor of Burnaby, Bill Copeland, announced that from June 12 to June 25 he would proclaim B.C. Old Age Pensioners, Senior Citizens and All Elder Citizens' Week. I am proud that my community has recognized the importance of seniors and chose this two-week period to concentrate on the issues and concerns facing senior citizens. Indeed, I hope the House will adopt this motion in time to designate the second Sunday in June this year as National Senior Citizens' Day which falls during that two-week period suggested by the mayor of Burnaby.
When I speak of these groups, of course there are similar groups throughout Canada, including in Edmonton, Winnipeg and many other areas. I speak now of the B.C. Old Age Pensioners Organization. I am always pleased to meet with representatives of that organization, people like Bill Anderson, Mildred McKay, and certainly their hard-working secretary, Delphine Carroll. The Burnaby Health Department, along with health departments throughout Canada, sponsors a volunteer section which provides shopping and banking services for seniors as well as volunteers to accompany them on walks or simply have a telephone conversation. The Edmonds Community Centre recently received New Horizons grant funding to run the Retired Health Watch Program. I had the honour of presenting a cheque to that group so they could continue this important work.
Similarly, the Burnaby Seniors Peer Counselling Service offers counselling to senior citizens in Burnaby who are experiencing the normal difficulties in life. These are seniors in the community who have completed a training program and are chosen for their warmth, sensitivity and life experiences. I would hope similar programs would be developed across Canada.
Other New Horizons grants which have gone recently to my constituency include one to the Bonsor seniors of Burnaby who requested a contribution for their program of recreational activities. Then there was the New Outlook group based at the Swedish Senior Citizens Home which got a contribution to establish a gardening program. Telecare Burnaby Senior Services assist with a support and information referral service for those in need. The New Vista Seniors Bowlers involves a program of carpet bowling. Finally there is a group called the Use It or Lose It group in Burnaby which just received a contribution to enhance a variety of outdoor sports activities at the Cameron Community Centre.
There is much that is being done in the community and many important services are being offered. However, there still remain concerns. There is the question of telephones and the Post Office, vital services for seniors in keeping in contact with relatives and friends and remaining active in volunteer work. It is therefore essential that the Government consider seniors when it increases postal rates and pursues a policy which may jeopardize door-to-door delivery. In my own riding, for
National Senior Citizens' Day
example, on too many occasions the Post Office has removed postal boxes without even consulting seniors affected by the decision. Seniors are also very concerned across Canada about the possibility of telephone companies such as B.C. Tel and Bell Canada implementing Local Measured Service which would mean charges for individual calls. My colleague from Beaches spoke about this on a number of occasions. It is a policy which flies in the face of the concept of universal access to telephones. I have tabled many petitions on behalf of the residents of Burnaby with respect to this issue.
Other concerns include the question of taxation. We in the NDP have long called for a fair tax system. Our most recent figures show that 8,000 Canadians with incomes in excess of $50,000 paid not one penny in income tax. Another 250 Canadians with incomes in excess of $250,000 did not pay a cent in income tax. That is unacceptable. That increases the burden on senior citizens and other ordinary Canadians. Frank Helden, for example, a senior in my constituency has raised concerns about the fact that the small pension he receives is taxed at the source. Surely that is unjust and unacceptable.
Another group of seniors who should be recognized for their contribution to our community and country is our veterans. This is done in an outstanding way in many cases by the Canadian Legion. I have two branches of the Legion in my constituency, the South Burnaby Branch, No. 83, and the North Burnaby Branch. Certainly they do a terrific job. However, veterans from World War 1, World War II, the Korean War, indeed veterans who volunteered to fight in the Spanish Civil War, the Mac-Paps, of which I understand some 100 are still living in Canada, fought for democracy and deserve recognition. We have called on the Government to recognize their contribution. Other seniors volunteered for combat duty but were never called to serve overseas. We believe they should be entitled to be treated with justice, fairness and equity. That is a promise the Government made which remains unfulfilled.
Finally, with respect to housing, there is no doubt many seniors would like to live on their own but are prevented from doing so because of the lack of affordable and accessible housing. Seniors want to live independently and with dignity. Recently I participated in the opening of Douglas Manor in Burnaby, named after Tommy Douglas, of course. That is another example of the tremendous work done by the New Vista society in Burnaby. The goal of that society in striving for an integrated living system for seniors is essential to our communities. They have, for example, special facilities for the disabled. That is the kind of concept we want to encourage everywhere in our society. I had the pleasure of opening the new wing of Douglas Manor with other officials recently and I could only think of how civilized it would be if all our seniors could live independently in such well-constructed, well-designed and well-maintained facilities. It is truly a great tribute to Tommy Douglas.
Finally, there is another sadder part of the story. We recognize that seniors in communities have contributed an

April 18, 1988
National Senior Citizens' Day
enormous amount to our society. The purpose of this motion is to recognize the contribution they have made. It is clear that we have forgotten about too many of them with regard to such things as pensions and housing. It is unfortunate, as well, but we must remember that the vast majority of seniors who live in poverty are women. In 1984, 59 per cent of single elderly women lived on an income of less than $9,000 per year. That was well below the poverty level set by the National Council on Welfare. In 1981, 14 per cent of the men over 65 were widowed while 49 per cent of women were. We must look seriously at eliminating this inequality and bringing about meaningful pension reform which addresses the very serious problems faced by elderly women in particular in our society.
As I said, this motion is important. It is important, both in terms of action and in terms of symbolism, to recognize the outstanding contribution which senior citizens have made to our society in the past and will continue to make in the future.
Probably the most important legacy that a society can leave is a world of peace and disarmament. I know that groups such as Veterans Against Nuclear Arms and other seniors across Canada are deeply concerned that Canadians reaffirm our commitment to peace, disarmament, development, and a more just distribution of wealth globally. In fact, this Saturday, April 23, in Vancouver I will be joining with, I hope, tens of thousands of people, many of them elderly, in the annual Walk for Peace. Seniors will be walking for peace for their children and for their children's children.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the House will recognize the importance of this motion which is not a partisan issue. I hope that Members on all sides of the House in all Parties will join together in agreeing to consider seriously this important issue of recognizing the tremendous work and the tremendous contribution of senior citizens in Canada and designating the second Sunday in June of each year as National Senior Citizens' Day.
As the Member of Parliament for Burnaby and a member of the New Democratic Party caucus I am proud to bring this motion before the House. I hope that it will be approved unanimously by all Members.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dan McKenzie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SENIOR CITIZENS' DAY DESIGNATION OF NATIONAL DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be the lead speaker for the government side on the motion before us today. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, I have had the honour to take part in a number of seniors-related discussions and activities. I can tell the House that the Minister's interest in and commitment to seniors is no less than his very well known commitment to veterans.
Hon. Members will recall that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appointed the Minister as Canada's first Minister of State for Seniors in August of last year. This appointment
was a very important watershed in the Progressive Conservative Party's long and distinguished record of caring and commitment toward seniors. It is a tradition which we in this Party build on day by day. The significance of the appointment of a Minister of State for Seniors should not be underestimated. Seniors themselves certainly do not.
For the first time seniors have a Minister who is mandated to represent their interests at the cabinet table and in government. They also have, as the Minister himself describes it, a "friend at court" to speak out on their behalf, to help cut red tape, and to simplify their dealings with the Government. If seniors need help, they know they can always count on George to provide it.
Finally, seniors have a Minister who is actively to seek their thoughts and ideas and to make those views known to the appropriate line Ministers. We have already seen the effectiveness of this role with the announcement of the seniors initiative on February 9. I will touch on that later in my remarks.
Consequently, in considering what can and should be done on behalf of Canadian seniors it should first be recognized that the appointment of a seniors Minister is a very major accomplishment. All of us on the government benches are proud of the development and I can assure the House that seniors are delighted as well. Fundamental to the success of a seniors Minister is that he or she be in touch with the views of the people being represented. The current Minister is firmly dedicated to that principle and he has often said that seniors are the ones setting the priorities. This was exactly the course the Minister followed with veterans, and with considerable success.
Over the past several months the Minister has heard from over 2,500 seniors and seniors' organizations. First-class ideas have come forward and the Minister has been actively reviewing these proposals. The Minister has also been asking seniors for their views on specific questions so as to enable them to best represent their interests in government.
In keeping with this approach, it very much seems to me that this motion is premature. Instead of barging ahead with a motion or referring the subject matter to a parliamentary committee, we should have some assurance that seniors themselves feel that this is an idea worth priority call on our time and efforts. This raises an interesting question and I tend to believe, Mr. Speaker, that seniors would prefer that we concentrate on initiatives similar to the seniors' initiatives announced this February.
I say this because the seniors' initiative was tailored to the priority items raised with the Minister of State for Seniors during his consultations. These items reflect the areas of importance to seniors and are worth reviewing to provide a point of comparison with the motion before us today.
The first component is the seniors' independence program. It is an entirely new program designed to improve the quality of life and independence of seniors. I am very excited about this
April 18, 1988

initiative because it will help keep seniors in their own homes, where they are far happier, and out of institutions. Twenty million dollars a year will be made available for projects approved under this program.
Increased support for the New Horizons program was the second component of the seniors initiative. This program has helped thousands of seniors to develop resources, services, and opportunities that will benefit themselves and their communities. Some $8 million a year has been provided. This will rise to $15 million a year by 1989-90.
The third element on which I would like to touch is a less happy one. As too many Canadians are personally aware, the devastation caused by Alzheimer's disease is horrendous. There is no known cure and seniors are the chief victims. At least 300,000 Canadians suffer from Alzheimer's disease and many more, primarily family members, suffer along with those stricken by the disease. A research fund of $4 million annually has been established to focus on Alzheimer's as well as osteoporosis, both of which are serious impediments to independent living.
These initiatives are important, imaginative, and innovative, just like the people we are here to serve. However, this is only the beginning. The Minister has embarked on a second round of consultations and he is counting on seniors, their representatives, and parliamentarians to provide the help and advice needed to plan for tomorrow and beyond.
Knowing the Minister, he will want to follow up on this motion, as well as the one sponsored by Senator Croll, to see how seniors themselves feel about a national day or week in their honour. Further speakers may wish to elaborate on this point but I would be very concerned about intruding, or appearing to intrude, in an area that has largely been provincial in nature. Discussions with the provinces are a must in my opinion.
Another concern which I believe would be shared by all Members of Parliament is the fact that seniors are a diverse group with tremendously different backgrounds, goals and aspirations. We see this every day in our constituency office meetings, our mail, and our conversations. Consequently, what is it we wish to celebrate in a national seniors' day? Is it to celebrate the attainment of an arbitrary age or retirement status? It is easy enough to say that we want to acknowledge the outstanding achievements of seniors in building this country, but it is far more difficult to define the segment of the population we wish to recognize.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I would recommend that we follow the Minister's philosophy and, indeed, the Government's philosophy of letting seniors speak for themselves on this question. Let us seek out the views of our constituents. Let them bring forward their thoughts on the advisability of a national seniors' day. If we truly believe, as this Government does, that one listens and then acts, we will not proceed with a motion that has had only limited discussion among seniors and seniors' organizations.
National Senior Citizens' Day
I, for one, have no hesitation in waiting until the seniors in my riding have had a chance to consider this proposal.

Why have a National Senior Citizens Day? It seems so obvious to me. We have Mother's Day and we have Father's Day. Why have Mother's Day since we should celebrate our mothers every day? Why have Father's Day since we ought to celebrate our fathers every day. And what about Secretaries' Week, which is this week, unless I am mistaken? Why? It should be all year long. The reason is that we want to call people's attention more specifically at a certain time during the year to a group or a commemoration, such as the one which will be held on a coming Sunday, on April 24th, here on Parliament Hill, between twelve and one o'clock. The day will be devoted to the commemoration of the Armenians' massacre, or the Armenian genocide. Why on the 24th? We know the facts.
Therefore why should a day be set aside to acknowledge the outstanding contribution of our seniors to the development of Canada? This is because the more we age the more unfortunately our communities neglect their seniors. We forget them. I ride the subway in Montreal, I do not drive a car and I often see older people sitting there who are sadly looking at me. I look back and smile at them. This is not difficult. And suddenly I see their face alter and they often tell me: "You were quite nice, you smiled at me". You know that according to a saying, nobody needs more to smile than the one who has no reason to be smiling. So, I smile, because it is a nice gesture.
