Mr. Speaker, for the fourth time since last summer I take the floor to speak about those forgotten Canadians who work for the minimum wage. They are so forgotten that Statistics Canada and the Department of Labour do not know how many under federal jurisdiction are living on the minimum wage. It is an indication of how minimal is the interest in the minimum wage.

April 18, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Their lot is hard enough in most provinces but harder still in industries under federal jurisdiction such as railways, airlines, shipping companies, radio stations, television channels, and telecommunications. It is harder because in so many instances-indeed in all but one-the federal rate is lower.
The hardship they endure, however, is due not only to the wage being so low-$4 per hour-it is due also in the way inflation is outstripping their wages. These are wages which are earned by low paid, unskilled, unorganized, and largely forgotten workers.
The last federal minimum wage increase was in May, 1986, almost two years ago. Since that time the Consumer Price Index has gone up over 8 per cent so that the $4 per hour of 1986 are now worth only $3.84 in 1988. It was little enough in 1986, impossibly low in 1988.
It is time, and over time, that this wage rate were reviewed and improved. I submit, as I did in raising this subject, that the solution must include not only raising the federal minimum wage but indexing it according to the Consumer Price Index.
That is done, is it not, Mr. Speaker, for old age security pensions? It is done for Canada pensions. It is done for public service pensions. It is done for parliamentary pensions. Why is it so impossible for us to consider doing the same for those who need it most?
This proposal is not any wildcat radical notion. It has been practised in France since 1952. It was recommended in the United States by the Minimum Wage Study Commission and the General Accounting Office in 1983. It is not an irresponsible notion that surfaces in Private Members' Hour or in the Adjournment Debate. It is demonstrably a reasonable proposal put forward and practised by major Governments.
I am aware that some economists argue against minimum wages at all. I submit that that is not the issue. To raise the point at all is really to be irrelevant. The fact is we have the minimum wage. We have it in every jurisdiction in Canada, federally, provincially, and territorially.
The issue becomes: Is the minimum wage adequate to the need. Is it keeping pace with the cost of living? Is it providing protection to those who need it most, those who do not have other advocacy than this Parliament can afford? I am speaking about people who do not have any trade unions to speak for them or any hired agents, high-priced lawyers negotiating contracts for them. These are people who have to look to where I am speaking. They have to look to Parliament. They have to look to the House of Commons to bring before the representatives of the people of Canada, and through them the people themselves, the need of those who are otherwise without a voice.
I think of people who are struggling to make do on this kind of minimum wage, not only those who receive it under the federal jurisdiction but those who receive it in provincial and territorial industries. I am impressed at how impossible their plight is, especially when I think of what it costs to put a roof
over one's head, the roof of just one rented room, or perhaps two or three rooms in a basement apartment in the riding of Scarborough West or some other part of Metro Toronto.
I see why we have the arrival and the apparent though tragic permanency of food banks, for housing today is costing such a percentage of anyone's income that when a person's income is minimal the result is impossible without supplementary assistance.
I ask the Government to expedite its consideration of this matter and, if possible, to take the second step of indexing this wage so that in the future workers will not have to wait until officials get around to considering them, but like Members of Parliament, like pensioners, they will automatically receive their just due.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Hon. Member for his comments and for his concern for the plight of the working poor.
Since the Government took office it has increased the federal adult minimum wage from $3.50 to $4 per hour, an increase of 14 per cent. Also, given its potential conflict with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the lower youth rate was eliminated, augmenting the federal minimum wage for workers under the age of 17 to the adult rate, an increase of 23 per cent.
Labour Canada is constantly monitoring the status of the federal minimum wage. This monitoring takes into account such factors as changes in the rate of inflation, shifts in the unemployment rate, general economic conditions, and minimum wage rates in other jurisdictions.
As was indicated the last time the Hon. Member raised this issue, the most recent percentage increases in the federal minimum wage are above the rise in the Consumer Price Index since the Government took office in September, 1984. Thus, the purchasing power of minimum wage earners has been protected during the Government's mandate. Moreover, the federal rate remains at the median of the provincial rates.
On the specific issue of automatic indexation of the minimum wage versus periodic reviews, the Government and indeed all provincial and territorial Governments across Canada have until now taken the approach of periodically reviewing their minimum wage policy, rather than binding themselves to automatic increases that may or may not have a detrimental effect on the potential employment of minimum wage earners.
Minimum wage earners, and indeed all Canadian workers, have benefited from the Government's successful battle against inflation. Since 1984, inflation has remained in check despite very impressive rates of growth in the national economy and in the number of jobs created. All Canadian workers, including
April 18, 1988

those working at minimum wage, will benefit from a controlled inflation rate and the creation of new employment possibilities.
In conclusion, I wish to state that the Government will continue to monitor the situation of minimum wage earners and their economic prospects. As the Minister previously indicated to the Hon. Member, a review is presently under way which will be completed shortly. I can assure the Hon. Member that the Minister will take into account the Hon. Member's concerns in the examination of the results of that review.

Mr. Speaker, on February 10, 1988, I asked the Hon. Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) the following question: Why did the Department accept a truck designed and patented by a non-NATO country when there was an opportunity to get a "made-in-North America" truck to any specifications desired?
The Hon. Associate Minister of National Defence replied:
-on June 6, 1986, an interdepartmental force, which was later confirmed by the Ministers, decided to open up the bidding to all truck manufacturers in the world and not restrict it to NATO trucks.
At that time when the tenders were put out on July 31, 1986, all truck manufacturers, both inside and outside NATO, had an equal opportunity to meet the specifications.
When a truck was purchased, we purchased the lower priced truck of those trucks which met specifications. A couple of trucks did not meet specifications.
I wish to make the following comments. First, this was a wonderful opportunity to secure a truck to the specifications set out by the Department that could have been designed and made to those standards in Canada.
It would not then have been necessary to think about patents or technology that belonged to another country. Bombardier was one firm prepared to do this if sufficient time had been given, and possibly other Canadian firms would have come up with a vehicle. Then we would have had a Canadian or North American vehicle that perhaps would have cost less. This opportunity has now been lost. While the Department is satisfied with the truck that it has purchased it is still not and never will be a Canadian made truck as its technology rests in another land.
Second, the original press release stated that the new truck will be manufactured by the Urban Transportation Development Corporation (UTDC) Inc., Kingston, Ontario. Actually Lavalin Inc. of Montreal owns 85 per cent of UTDC, and the balance is owned by the provincial Government of Ontario. The trucks are now going to be built in Ontario. The contract is expected to generate some 500 jobs over a 24-month period and a large number of jobs after that.
Third, it is a shame, indeed, that the vehicles required are not to be manufactured in either western Canada under the Western Diversification Program or in the Maritimes. One
Adjournment Debate
firm, Bombardier, would have done the manufacturing in Cochrane, Alberta and would have used the entire western provinces for purchasing supplies. This would have added much to the economy of the West, had consideration been given to disparities. The Minister had advised that, in accordance with the government procurement guidelines no consideration could be given to regional disparities during the evaluation process.
It is my view that every contract let by the Government of Canada should consider regional disparities, and the guidelines should be so amended. This contract was let in Ontario where there is buoyancy in the economy, whereas in both the West and the Maritimes unemployment is rampant and both need industries that will be there for a long time. We missed this opportunity to secure an industry in the West that would have provided a great deal of diversification for many years to come.
Fourth, another matter of concern in this contract is the patent. I have been advised that Lavalin Inc. secured full rights to this vehicle. Is there a patent on the entire vehicle, and also on parts of the vehicle, that may spring up once the vehicle is constructed? It appears that the Government paid Lavalin $116,000 for the technology. I hope that all legal questions of ownership, patents, copyrights, et cetera, have been cleared so there can be no future trouble or cost to the Canadian people.
Fifth, the contract actually included seven types of trucks based on a common cab and chassis. There may be good reasons why these seven types of trucks had to be included in one contract, but, again, had this been broken down, there is always the possibility that a better price could have been secured and the work could have been spread across the country.
Sixth, there is also the matter of parts for the said vehicles. When 122 heavy trucks are being purchased, there should be a requirement that the manufacturer keep on hand a large supply of every part that may wear out or eventually have to be replaced. Certainly the grease, oil, and diesel fuel are standard, but there are some very serious questions about many truck parts that could wear out when lives are being threatened. I believe Lavalin should be required, with no ands, ifs, or buts, to keep all parts that may wear out in ready supply. It is not good enough to say that there might be other NATO trucks that have similar transmissions, similar cargo boxes, similar dump trucks, and similar carburetors.
I and the people of Cochrane, and indeed the people of western Canada, were bitterly disappointed when Bombardier lost this contract. Part of the hurt was salved when the Department of National Defence stated that, even when the present contract has been completed, there will still be a shortage of some 2,500 trucks. The splendid buildings in Cochrane, Alberta are still available. The people are anxious to welcome Bombardier, a Quebec firm to our province. It will strengthen unity of the nation. The firm would have an

April 18, 1988
Adjournment Debate
opportunity to expand its market to western Canada and the western U.S. states, and the diversification resulting would meet the requirements of the Western Diversification Program.
Cochrane stands ready to assist our military to secure the best equipment possible if given the opportunity. May the next tender come soon, and I hope the people of Cochrane will have reasons to cheer when the contract is let.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Price (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member must be congratulated for his vigorous defence of his constituents.
In February, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) announced that UTDC of Kingston would manufacture 1,122 heavy trucks at an approximate cost of $250 million. As the Hon. Member knows, there is a competitive bidding process, and in July of 1986, our request for proposal was sent to 13 Canadian companies. In March of 1987, responses were received from four companies.
In the request for proposal, the prospective bidders were advised that the final selection would be based on an aggregate assessment of five factors: one, the over-all cost to the Crown; two, compliance of the vehicle and its variants with the specification and the bidder proposed project management; three, industrial benefit; four, compliance of the Integrated Logistic Support System; and five, delivery.
An evaluation plan was prepared prior to receipt of the proposals and, as a part of the evaluation, candidate vehicles from the four bidders were acquired for technical and user trials. The results of these trials were incorporated into the final evaluation.
In August of 1987, the four bidders were requested to submit proposals for higher quantities because of the additional requirements arising from the White Paper. These proposals were received and separate evaluations were done by members of the Departments of National Defence, Regional Industrial Expansion, and Supply and Services. These results were consolidated into a final assessment and presented to an interdepartmental senior review board in January of this year and subsequently endorsed by Cabinet.
The awarding of this contract to UTDC ensures that Canada receives the optimum benefits in terms of excellence of equipment, Canadian content, industrial offsets, transfer of technology, employment, and value for money, and fully meets the requirements of the Canadian Forces.
